## Skills
A skill is a set of local instructions to follow that is stored in a `SKILL.md` file. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and a short path that can be expanded into an absolute path using the skill roots table.
### Skill roots
- `r0` = `/Users/pfleidi/.agents/skills`
- `r1` = `/Users/pfleidi/.codex/skills/.system`
- `r2` = `/Users/pfleidi/.codex/plugins/cache/openai-curated-remote`
### Available skills
- skill-creator: Create or update a Codex skill with appropriately scoped instructions and any needed supporting resources. (file: r1/skill-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-installer: Install Codex skills into $CODEX_HOME/skills from a curated list or a GitHub repo path. Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos). (file: r1/skill-installer/SKILL.md)
- context7-mcp: This skill should be used when the user asks about libraries, frameworks, API references, or needs code examples. Activates for setup questions, code generation involving libraries, or mentions of specific frameworks like React, Vue, Next.js, Prisma, Supabase, etc. (file: r0/context7-mcp/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:clean-go: Focused Go clean-code review and fix workflow for the current diff against origin/main, based on modern Go and local Go preferences. By default, fixes only high-confidence, unambiguous Required findings in one batch. Use when the user asks for clean Go review, Go cleanliness, Go refactoring review, pfleidi:clean-go, or when larger Go refactors/code changes need clean Go guidance. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/clean-go/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:daily-status: Use when the user asks for a daily Slack status, standup update, work recap, report since a previous update, or a summary of recent Linear, authored GitHub PR, Entire trail, and work-related Slack activity. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/daily-status/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:de-slop: Use when the user asks to de-slop, simplify code, remove cruft, reduce over-abstraction, clean up weak tests, simplify a current branch or named code area, or explicitly invokes pfleidi:de-slop. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/de-slop/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:explain-diff: Use when the user asks for a rich explanation, teaching-style walkthrough, or shareable writeup of a code change, diff, branch, commit, or PR — e.g. "explain this diff", "help me understand this PR", "make an explainer for this change" — or invokes /explain-diff. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/explain-diff/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:feedback: Use when the user asks to fix, address, explain, triage, respond to, dismiss, resolve, publish, or watch remote review feedback for the current branch; mentions Bugbot, Copilot, GitHub PR comments, or Entire trail findings; or invokes /feedback or pfleidi:feedback. Also collects read-only local findings alongside remote intake. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/feedback/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:guided-research: Use when the user asks for guided research, deep research, codebase understanding, a coworker-readable research artifact, answers to annotated research docs, or live watching of a Markdown research artifact. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/guided-research/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:investigate-alert: Use when the user provides a Datadog monitor URL/ID, Datadog event URL, pasted alert text, incident, or monitor name and asks whether it is noise, why it fired, how to investigate it, how to tune it, or invokes /investigate-alert. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/investigate-alert/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:pr: Use when the user wants to create, open, or make a GitHub pull request for the current branch, asks to prepare the branch for PR creation, provides an optional PR target base branch, or invokes /pr. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/pr/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:project-shape: Use when the user wants to investigate, define, or substantially restructure a multi-issue engineering project; turn a parent issue into thin vertical slices; identify spikes, dependencies, parallel work, risks, or completion criteria; or invokes project-shape. Do not use for a routine morning project reconciliation when project-update applies. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/project-shape/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:project-update: Use for a fast morning or recurring update of an existing multi-issue engineering project: reconcile material issue and pull-request changes, findings, blockers, flags, rollout or validation state; propose tracker corrections; record a concise parent update; and prioritize the next five meaningful steps. Do not use for initial project design or substantial restructuring when project-shape applies. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/project-update/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:remote-review: Use when the user asks for local feedback on a GitHub PR or Entire trail, provides a PR/trail URL or number, asks to review an Entire trail, asks for PR/trail feedback without fixing it, or explicitly invokes pfleidi:remote-review. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/remote-review/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:review: Use when the user asks to review the current branch, review a local diff, audit code changes before merge, run a code review or full review, or invokes /review. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/review/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:task-align: Align a single Linear or GitHub task before execution by verifying the problem, separating facts from proposals, settling material decisions, and defining development and post-deploy validation. Use when issue-derived work has unclear evidence, scope, behavior, risk, or validation, or when task-implement requests alignment. Skip clear, small tasks with no material decisions. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/task-align/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:task-implement: Start and implement one well-scoped Linear or GitHub task: align it when needed, update native tracker state, run no-code work in a coordinator-workspace tab, or create an Entire worktree and focused implementation session when repository changes are required. Use Herdr when active; otherwise use the invoking session. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/task-implement/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:task-validate: Perform isolated final validation of one implemented Linear or GitHub task against its live exit criteria and the full approved commit range. Use a temporary Entire worktree and, when already under Herdr, a dedicated validation tab and agent that can report code failures to the implementation agent. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/task-validate/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:testing: Local testing strategy and review guidance for meaningful tests, choosing unit vs integration vs end-to-end scope, avoiding production-only test seams and over-mocking, and keeping test helpers readable, especially in Go. Use when writing, changing, or reviewing tests; adding mocks or test helpers; deciding test scope; or when user mentions pfleidi:testing. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/testing/SKILL.md)
- plugin-management:plugin-management: Discover and suggest relevant plugins, inspect app permissions and dependencies, and manage plugin connections or removal. Use when the user asks about plugins or when a task would materially benefit from an external app, account, service, or data source that available tools cannot access. (file: r2/plugin-management/0.1.0/skills/plugin-management/SKILL.md)
- search: Use when the user wants to find prior work, checkpoints, or agent conversations by topic, repo, branch, author, or recent time window, or to search code content across repositories (file: r0/search/SKILL.md)
- using-entire: Use when codebase exploration or explanation would benefit from historical implementation intent recorded in Entire checkpoints. Combines current source with checkpoint evidence without treating unavailable history as a blocker. (file: r0/using-entire/SKILL.md)

---
name: task-implement
description: >
  Start and implement one well-scoped Linear or GitHub task: align it when
  needed, update native tracker state, run no-code work in a
  coordinator-workspace tab, or create an Entire worktree and focused
  implementation session when repository changes are required. Use Herdr when
  active; otherwise use the invoking session.
---

# Task Implementation

Move one well-scoped task from ready to active implementation while keeping the
tracker authoritative and the implementation context focused. Do not create an
Entire trail by default.

## Preflight

Before changing tracker state:

- Resolve the live task, repository, repository parent, current user, and task
  tracker access.
- Use Herdr enhancements only when `HERDR_ENV=1` and the Herdr CLI is available.
  Otherwise use the direct fallback; Herdr must not block the core workflow.

After preflight succeeds, assign the task to the user and move it to the
tracker's native in-progress state.

## Choose Each Herdr Agent

Apply this immediately before every new `herdr agent start` performed by this
skill. Do not ask when resuming an existing live agent or when Herdr is absent.

Resolve the agent kind currently running this skill from the coordinator's live
Herdr agent. If it cannot be resolved, stop rather than guessing the timeout
default. After the role-specific workflow creates the destination tab and pane,
leave its shell idle. Use that shell to show a visible choice between Codex
(`codex`) and Claude Code (`claude`), focus the chooser, and send a Herdr
notification with the request sound. Wait up to 300 seconds for `c`/`codex` or
`l`/`claude`.

If the user does not answer within 300 seconds, select the coordinator's current
agent kind. An invalid answer does not select an agent; keep asking within the
original deadline. Have the shell print the selected canonical Herdr kind, wait
for the shell prompt to return, and pass that value to `herdr agent start
--kind`. The choice applies only to this dispatch; ask again before the next new
agent. Compare only the fixed accepted tokens; never evaluate the user's input
as shell text. Keep the timed read running in the destination pane and poll for
its result at intervals no longer than 60 seconds. Record each selected kind in
the live `Herdr peers` block, not the issue.

## Align

Use `pfleidi:task-align` unless the live task is already clear enough to execute
without first settling what work is being requested. Skip explicit alignment
only when all of these are true:

- The desired outcome, scope, exit criteria, and applicable validation are
  concrete and mutually consistent.
- Current evidence does not call the task's premise or requested change into
  question.
- Execution requires either no repository edits or only a few obvious code or
  configuration lines with no meaningful design choice.
- The task is not high-risk, destructive, broad, or dependent on a shared
  contract or maintenance direction that still needs agreement.

Operational validation, telemetry dashboard changes, small configuration
edits, well-scoped decision or investigation tasks, and similarly narrow work
commonly qualify. Their type alone is not enough: align when the issue leaves a
consequential prerequisite choice unresolved. Alignment should not perform the
decision or investigation that constitutes the task itself. When skipping
alignment, do not create an alignment tab, agent, or comment; use the live task
as the handoff and continue directly to path selection.

When running under Herdr, load its current agent instructions with
`herdr --skill`. Capture the coordinator workspace, tab, and pane from the
injected Herdr environment and resolve the current pane's live agent target.
Do not rely on UI focus.

Derive the applicable task agent names once. Lowercase the task ID, replace each
run of characters outside `[a-z0-9_-]` with `_`, prefix it with `align_`,
`task_`, `impl_`, or `validate_`, and truncate the complete name to 32
characters. Treat these as expected names: list live agents, reject ambiguous
collisions, and resume an existing name only after verifying that its pane and
workspace own this task. Do not add a suffix or create a registry file.

When alignment is required, create an ephemeral alignment tab in the
coordinator workspace with its working directory set to the repository parent.
Capture the returned tab and root-pane IDs, run the per-dispatch choice, and
start the alignment agent as `align_<task-id>` with the selected kind. Its
initial prompt must contain a `Herdr peers` block with:

- the task ID;

alignment, do not create an alignment tab, agent, or comment; use the live task
as the handoff and continue directly to path selection.

When running under Herdr, load its current agent instructions with
`herdr --skill`. Capture the coordinator workspace, tab, and pane from the
injected Herdr environment and resolve the current pane's live agent target.
Do not rely on UI focus.

Derive the applicable task agent names once. Lowercase the task ID, replace each
run of characters outside `[a-z0-9_-]` with `_`, prefix it with `align_`,

characters. Treat these as expected names: list live agents, reject ambiguous
collisions, and resume an existing name only after verifying that its pane and
workspace own this task. Do not add a suffix or create a registry file.

When alignment is required, create an ephemeral alignment tab in the
coordinator workspace with its working directory set to the repository parent.

start the alignment agent as `align_<task-id>` with the selected kind. Its
initial prompt must contain a `Herdr peers` block with:

- the alignment agent's actual name, kind, tab ID, and pane ID;
- the expected no-code task, implementation, and validation names and roles.

Let the user conduct alignment in that tab. The alignment agent reports the
comment link and completion or blocker state to the coordinator target. The
coordinator waits for the agent to settle and reads its output before proceeding.
Keep the tab open while alignment is active or paused. For the code-change path,
keep it until implementation acknowledges the handoff; the no-code path closes
it as described below.

Without Herdr, perform required alignment in the invoking session. Skip tab
creation, peer-agent identity, and inter-agent communication.

If alignment shows that the task is blocked or not ready, do not create a
worktree. Reflect the outcome using the tracker's native state and the concise
alignment comment rather than a parallel status record.

## Choose The Execution Path

Use the live exit criteria and any alignment result to decide whether completion
requires repository edits and a commit. If the answer is unclear, run alignment
before creating a branch or worktree.

For a decision, investigation, tracker-only change, operational validation, or
other task that requires no repository change:

- Do not resolve a branch name, invoke Entire, create a worktree or task
  workspace, or start implementation or validation agents.
- Under Herdr, create a new tab in the existing coordinator workspace with its
  working directory set to the repository parent and label it for the task.
  Capture its returned tab and pane IDs and start a fresh `task_<task-id>` agent
  there using the per-dispatch agent choice. Do not create another workspace.
- Prompt that agent with the live task, the alignment comment when one exists,
  and a `Herdr peers` block containing the coordinator and no-code task agents'
  actual targets, kinds, and IDs, plus the alignment agent when one was used.
  Require it to acknowledge the handoff to the coordinator before closing any
  alignment tab.
- Have the no-code task agent perform the work without editing repository files
  or creating commits, then report completion or blockers to the coordinator.
  The coordinator waits for it to settle and reads its output before closing
  the tab. Keep the tab open when user input is still required.
- Without Herdr, continue the work in the invoking session.
- In either path, use the issue's exit criteria as the completion contract.
- Persist durable findings and decisions in the issue, and use native tracker
  state for completion or follow-up work.

For an explicit staging or production validation task, exercise only supported
customer behavior: public API requests from a script, browser-driven web UI
flows, or normal CLI commands. Verify that the deployed system is wired
together and produces the customer-visible result. Do not connect to production
databases or internal services, inject faulty queue messages, manufacture
internal failures, or use privileged mechanisms unavailable to a customer.

Keep edge cases, failure injection, and critical correctness checks local and
prefer automated coverage executed in CI. If deployed validation exposes a
missing case that requires internal access to reproduce, record it and
reclassify the necessary automated test or code change rather than attempting
that case against staging or production.

changes. If no-code work discovers that a code change is required, stop, record
the evidence, notify the coordinator, and reclassify the task before entering
the code-change path. Do not edit repository files from the no-code tab.

## Prepare Code Work

Only when repository changes are required:

- Confirm the Entire CLI is available and the repository supports Entire
  worktrees.
- Look for an existing branch, worktree, pull request, or Entire trail for the
  task. Resume the matching work instead of creating a duplicate. If ownership
  or intent is unclear, stop with the conflicting evidence.
- For Linear, read and use the issue's suggested branch name exactly. For a
  GitHub issue without an existing or suggested branch, ask the user for the
  branch name instead of inventing a convention.
- Reject an empty or option-like branch name. Validate it with `git
  check-ref-format --branch`, then pass it to Entire as one quoted argument.

For the code-change path, use Entire to create one worktree for the validated
task branch. `entire worktree create <branch>` creates and checks out a new
branch; use its existing-branch mode only when preparation established that the
matching branch already exists. Pass the branch as one quoted argument.

Do not use `git worktree`, create a trail, remove the implementation worktree,
or touch any other worktree. Record the path returned by Entire.

## Start Implementation

For the code-change path, when running under Herdr:

- Create a task-specific workspace rooted at the implementation worktree and
  capture its returned workspace, root-tab, and root-pane IDs.
- Keep that root tab as the shell tab. Create an implementation-agent tab and
  capture its returned tab and pane IDs.
- Start the implementation agent with the already reserved `impl_<task-id>`
  name and the per-dispatch agent choice. If that name became occupied, verify
  it owns this task or stop.
- Prompt the agent with the live task link, the alignment comment link when one
  exists, the implementation worktree and branch, and the task-specific
  request. Tell it to re-read the live issue before acting.
- Include a `Herdr peers` block with the coordinator's actual target, kind, and
  workspace ID, the implementation agent's actual name, kind, workspace, tab,
  and pane IDs, the reserved validation name, and the alignment agent's name,
  kind, and tab ID when one was used. This block is live session context, not a
  tracker record.
- Require the implementation agent to acknowledge the handoff to the exact
  coordinator target. The coordinator reads that acknowledgment before closing
  any alignment tab and exiting.

scoped to the returned worktree. Do not synthesize agent identities or attempt
message forwarding.

Follow the repository's normal checkpoint, testing, and commit-approval rules.
The task's live exit criteria are the completion contract. Alignment comments
and implementation summaries provide context but cannot silently add, remove,
or weaken criteria.

## Persist Discoveries

When task work reveals a durable constraint, edge case, corrected fact, or
user-approved change of direction, update the relevant issue field or add a
concise issue comment. Start agent-generated handoff comments with the required
repository marker. Keep ordinary progress, branch state, and pull-request state
in their native tracker fields and links.

Do not copy session conversation into the tracker. Never mention internal
session-capture configuration in generated issue output or handoffs.

---
name: herdr
description: "Control Herdr, a terminal multiplexer for coding agents. Use only when the user explicitly mentions Herdr or asks to use Herdr to inspect or control panes, tabs, workspaces, commands, or another agent. Do not use merely because a task could benefit from a background terminal, delegation, or parallel work. Requires HERDR_ENV=1."
---

# Herdr

Herdr organizes terminals into workspaces, tabs, and panes, recognizes coding agents running inside panes, and exposes the current session through the `herdr` CLI.

Before issuing any control command, verify that this agent is running inside a Herdr-managed pane:

```bash
test "${HERDR_ENV:-}" = 1
```

If the check fails, say that you are not running inside Herdr and stop. Do not inspect or control the focused Herdr session from outside Herdr.

When the check passes, the `herdr` binary in `PATH` talks to the current session. Use it to inspect neighboring work, create terminal layout, start agents and commands, read output, and wait for state changes.

## Learn the current CLI

The installed binary is the authority for command syntax. Start with:

```bash
herdr --help
```

Then print the relevant command group by running the group without a subcommand:

```bash
herdr agent
herdr pane
herdr workspace
herdr tab
herdr worktree
herdr terminal
herdr notification
herdr integration
herdr session
```

Do not run bare `herdr` for discovery; it launches or attaches the TUI. Do not probe a mutating nested command by omitting arguments. Commands such as `herdr workspace create` are valid with defaults and will execute.

Most control commands return JSON. Read identifiers and state from those responses instead of predicting them.

## Understand layout, panes, and agents

Choose the primitive that matches the job:

- Workspace, tab, and pane topology organize terminal locations.
- Pane commands control raw terminals, shells, tests, servers, input, and output.
- Agent commands control the recognized coding agent currently occupying a pane.

A pane exists whether or not it contains an agent. `agent start` requires an existing available shell pane and never creates, splits, or moves layout. Use pane commands for ordinary processes. Use agent commands when Herdr must validate agent identity or interpret `idle`, `working`, `blocked`, `done`, and `unknown` lifecycle states.

Agent commands accept either a unique live agent name or the pane ID currently hosting that agent. They do not accept terminal IDs or bare agent-kind labels. Names must match `[a-z][a-z0-9_-]{0,31}` and be unique among live agents. A name follows the current pane occupant and is cleared when that agent exits, is released, or is replaced.

`idle` means the agent is ready for input and its tab has been seen in the focused Herdr UI. `done` is the same underlying idle state after unseen background work finishes. Focusing the tab or targeting the pane or agent with a focus command marks it seen. CLI reads do not mark it seen. `blocked` means Herdr recognized an approval or question UI. `unknown` means an agent is present but Herdr cannot classify it confidently; it does not prove completion.

## Use IDs and caller context

Public IDs are opaque stable handles:

- workspace: `w1`
- tab: `w1:t1`
- pane: `w1:p1`

Closed tab and pane IDs are not reused. A pane moved into another workspace receives a new workspace-qualified pane ID. After `pane move`, continue with `.result.move_result.pane.pane_id` or the live agent name. The old value is reported as `.result.move_result.previous_pane_id`; only the moved process's inherited caller context keeps resolving that old ID, so do not use it as a general agent target.

Herdr injects the caller's context into each managed pane:

```bash
printf '%s\n' "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID" "$HERDR_TAB_ID" "$HERDR_PANE_ID"
```

Prefer `--current` when a pane command should target the calling pane. Omitting a target may use the UI-focused pane, which can belong to the user or another client.

Discover live state with:

```bash
herdr workspace list
herdr tab list --workspace "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID"
herdr pane current --current
herdr pane list --workspace "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID"
herdr agent list
```

Creation responses expose the IDs to use next. `workspace create` returns `.result.workspace`, `.result.tab`, and `.result.root_pane`. `tab create` returns `.result.tab` and `.result.root_pane`. `pane split` returns the new pane as `.result.pane`.

## Start and coordinate an agent

Default to a sibling pane in the current tab and the current working directory. Do not create a workspace, tab, worktree, or different cwd unless the user explicitly requests that topology or location.

Honor a direction requested by the user. Otherwise inspect the caller pane:

```bash
herdr pane layout --pane "$HERDR_PANE_ID"
```

Split a wide pane to the right and a narrow or tall pane down. Avoid repeated same-direction splits that create unusably narrow columns or short rows. Keep the user's focus in the calling pane and explicitly preserve the caller's working directory:

```bash
herdr pane split --current --direction right --cwd "$PWD" --no-focus
```

Replace `right` with `down` when appropriate. Read the new pane ID from `.result.pane.pane_id`.

An available shell pane must be at its interactive prompt, with the shell itself in the foreground and no foreground command, editor, or agent running. Start a supported agent in that pane with a useful unique name:

```bash
herdr agent start reviewer --kind codex --pane <returned-pane-id>
```

Use the kind requested by the user. Run `herdr agent` to inspect the installed kind list and options. Pass native agent arguments only after `--`:

```bash
herdr agent start reviewer --kind codex --pane <returned-pane-id> -- <agent-args...>
```

A successful `agent start` returns only after Herdr detects the expected agent in the same pane and considers it ready for interactive input. If the agent is blocked during startup, the command returns `agent_not_ready` immediately but keeps the name available for `agent read` and `agent send-keys`. Wait until the agent becomes idle before prompting it. Startup defaults to a 30-second timeout.

Submit work through the agent surface:

```bash
herdr agent prompt reviewer "Review the current diff and report only actionable findings." --wait --timeout 120000
```

`agent prompt` honors the pane's live bracketed-paste mode and sends text followed by encoded Enter after a short delay. It rejects an agent already waiting at an approval or question dialog with `agent_blocked` before sending any input. Inspect the blocked UI and ask the user before answering it. For normal agent work, `--wait` is enough: it waits for the first settled `idle`, `done`, or `blocked` state. Do not repeat those defaults with `--until`.

A prompt sent from a non-working state must produce an observed lifecycle change within five seconds. Otherwise Herdr returns `agent_prompt_stalled` instead of waiting indefinitely. This wait tracks lifecycle state, not an individual turn; if the agent is already working, completion of the active turn may satisfy it.

Use `--until` only for a state-specific workflow, such as waiting for an already-running agent to request input:

```bash
herdr agent wait reviewer --until blocked --timeout 120000
```

Without `--until`, standalone `agent wait` uses the same settled-state defaults as `agent prompt --wait`.

Use logical keys for interactive agent UI controls:

```bash
herdr agent send-keys reviewer esc
herdr agent send-keys reviewer ctrl+c
```

Herdr validates all keys before writing any bytes. Read the result through the resolved agent:

```bash
herdr agent get reviewer
herdr agent read reviewer --source recent-unwrapped --lines 120
```

If a wait fails or returns `blocked`, inspect `agent get` and `agent read` before deciding what input to send. Use the pane surface only when raw terminal control is intentional.

## Run an ordinary command in another pane

Create a sibling pane with the same geometry rule, preserve the caller's working directory, and keep user focus unchanged:

```bash
herdr pane split --current --direction right --cwd "$PWD" --no-focus
```

Read the new pane ID from `.result.pane.pane_id`, then run and inspect the command:

```bash
herdr pane run <returned-pane-id> "just test"
herdr pane wait-output <returned-pane-id> --match "test result" --timeout 120000
herdr pane read <returned-pane-id> --source recent-unwrapped --lines 120
```

`pane run` atomically sends command text and Enter. `pane wait-output` searches the selected snapshot immediately, so output that already exists can match. Use `--match <text>` for a literal substring or `--regex <pattern>` for a Rust regular expression. Omitting `--timeout` allows an indefinite wait.

Use the read source that matches the task:

- `visible`: the currently rendered viewport.
- `recent`: recent rendered output, including soft wraps.
- `recent-unwrapped`: recent output with soft wraps joined; prefer it for logs and transcripts.
- `detection`: the plain-text bottom-buffer snapshot used for agent detection.

Use `--format ansi` when colors and terminal styling are evidence. Otherwise use text.

`--lines` asks Herdr for more rows from the pane's available screen and host scrollback. If increasing it does not reveal more of a completed response, the pane is probably running the agent on the terminal's alternate screen. Rows that leave the alternate screen do not enter Herdr's host scrollback, so a larger line count cannot recover them.

After that failed read, ask the agent to write its complete response as Markdown in a temporary directory and reply only with the file path, then read the file directly. Use this only as a fallback; do not request file output in the initial prompt.

## Safety and coordination rules

- Use `--no-focus` for background work unless the user asked to switch context.
- Use `--current`, an explicit pane ID, or a unique agent name. Do not rely on another client's focused pane.
- Parse IDs from JSON responses. Do not derive them from sidebar order or examples.
- Do not close workspaces, tabs, panes, or sessions you did not create unless the user explicitly asked.
- Never run `herdr server stop` from an active session unless the user explicitly intends to stop the server and its pane processes.
- Never kill the main Herdr process. Use named test sessions for experiments that need an isolated server.
- CLI server errors are JSON on stderr with exit status 1. CLI syntax errors exit with status 2.

description: "Control Herdr, a terminal multiplexer for coding agents. Use only when the user explicitly mentions Herdr or asks to use Herdr to inspect or control panes, tabs, workspaces, commands, or another agent. Do not use merely because a task could benefit from a background terminal, delegation, or parallel work. Requires HERDR_ENV=1."
---

# Herdr

Herdr organizes terminals into workspaces, tabs, and panes, recognizes coding agents running inside panes, and exposes the current session through the `herdr` CLI.

Before issuing any control command, verify that this agent is running inside a Herdr-managed pane:

```bash
test "${HERDR_ENV:-}" = 1
```

If the check fails, say that you are not running inside Herdr and stop. Do not inspect or control the focused Herdr session from outside Herdr.

When the check passes, the `herdr` binary in `PATH` talks to the current session. Use it to inspect neighboring work, create terminal layout, start agents and commands, read output, and wait for state changes.

## Learn the current CLI

The installed binary is the authority for command syntax. Start with:

```bash
herdr --help
```

Then print the relevant command group by running the group without a subcommand:

```bash
herdr agent
herdr pane
herdr workspace
herdr tab
herdr worktree
herdr terminal
herdr notification
herdr integration
herdr session
```

Do not run bare `herdr` for discovery; it launches or attaches the TUI. Do not probe a mutating nested command by omitting arguments. Commands such as `herdr workspace create` are valid with defaults and will execute.

Most control commands return JSON. Read identifiers and state from those responses instead of predicting them.

## Understand layout, panes, and agents

Choose the primitive that matches the job:

- Workspace, tab, and pane topology organize terminal locations.
- Pane commands control raw terminals, shells, tests, servers, input, and output.
- Agent commands control the recognized coding agent currently occupying a pane.

A pane exists whether or not it contains an agent. `agent start` requires an existing available shell pane and never creates, splits, or moves layout. Use pane commands for ordinary processes. Use agent commands when Herdr must validate agent identity or interpret `idle`, `working`, `blocked`, `done`, and `unknown` lifecycle states.

Agent commands accept either a unique live agent name or the pane ID currently hosting that agent. They do not accept terminal IDs or bare agent-kind labels. Names must match `[a-z][a-z0-9_-]{0,31}` and be unique among live agents. A name follows the current pane occupant and is cleared when that agent exits, is released, or is replaced.

`idle` means the agent is ready for input and its tab has been seen in the focused Herdr UI. `done` is the same underlying idle state after unseen background work finishes. Focusing the tab or targeting the pane or agent with a focus command marks it seen. CLI reads do not mark it seen. `blocked` means Herdr recognized an approval or question UI. `unknown` means an agent is present but Herdr cannot classify it confidently; it does not prove completion.

## Use IDs and caller context

Public IDs are opaque stable handles:

- workspace: `w1`
- tab: `w1:t1`
- pane: `w1:p1`

Closed tab and pane IDs are not reused. A pane moved into another workspace receives a new workspace-qualified pane ID. After `pane move`, continue with `.result.move_result.pane.pane_id` or the live agent name. The old value is reported as `.result.move_result.previous_pane_id`; only the moved process's inherited caller context keeps resolving that old ID, so do not use it as a general agent target.

Herdr injects the caller's context into each managed pane:

```bash
printf '%s\n' "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID" "$HERDR_TAB_ID" "$HERDR_PANE_ID"
```

Prefer `--current` when a pane command should target the calling pane. Omitting a target may use the UI-focused pane, which can belong to the user or another client.

Discover live state with:

```bash
herdr workspace list
herdr tab list --workspace "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID"
herdr pane current --current
herdr pane list --workspace "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID"
herdr agent list
```

Creation responses expose the IDs to use next. `workspace create` returns `.result.workspace`, `.result.tab`, and `.result.root_pane`. `tab create` returns `.result.tab` and `.result.root_pane`. `pane split` returns the new pane as `.result.pane`.

## Start and coordinate an agent

Default to a sibling pane in the current tab and the current working directory. Do not create a workspace, tab, worktree, or different cwd unless the user explicitly requests that topology or location.

Honor a direction requested by the user. Otherwise inspect the caller pane:

```bash
herdr pane layout --pane "$HERDR_PANE_ID"
```

Split a wide pane to the right and a narrow or tall pane down. Avoid repeated same-direction splits that create unusably narrow columns or short rows. Keep the user's focus in the calling pane and explicitly preserve the caller's working directory:

```bash
herdr pane split --current --direction right --cwd "$PWD" --no-focus
```

Replace `right` with `down` when appropriate. Read the new pane ID from `.result.pane.pane_id`.

An available shell pane must be at its interactive prompt, with the shell itself in the foreground and no foreground command, editor, or agent running. Start a supported agent in that pane with a useful unique name:

```bash
herdr agent start reviewer --kind codex --pane <returned-pane-id>
```

Use the kind requested by the user. Run `herdr agent` to inspect the installed kind list and options. Pass native agent arguments only after `--`:

```bash
herdr agent start reviewer --kind codex --pane <returned-pane-id> -- <agent-args...>
```

A successful `agent start` returns only after Herdr detects the expected agent in the same pane and considers it ready for interactive input. If the agent is blocked during startup, the command returns `agent_not_ready` immediately but keeps the name available for `agent read` and `agent send-keys`. Wait until the agent becomes idle before prompting it. Startup defaults to a 30-second timeout.

Submit work through the agent surface:

```bash
herdr agent prompt reviewer "Review the current diff and report only actionable findings." --wait --timeout 120000
```

`agent prompt` honors the pane's live bracketed-paste mode and sends text followed by encoded Enter after a short delay. It rejects an agent already waiting at an approval or question dialog with `agent_blocked` before sending any input. Inspect the blocked UI and ask the user before answering it. For normal agent work, `--wait` is enough: it waits for the first settled `idle`, `done`, or `blocked` state. Do not repeat those defaults with `--until`.

A prompt sent from a non-working state must produce an observed lifecycle change within five seconds. Otherwise Herdr returns `agent_prompt_stalled` instead of waiting indefinitely. This wait tracks lifecycle state, not an individual turn; if the agent is already working, completion of the active turn may satisfy it.

Use `--until` only for a state-specific workflow, such as waiting for an already-running agent to request input:

```bash
herdr agent wait reviewer --until blocked --timeout 120000
```

Without `--until`, standalone `agent wait` uses the same settled-state defaults as `agent prompt --wait`.

Use logical keys for interactive agent UI controls:

```bash
herdr agent send-keys reviewer esc
herdr agent send-keys reviewer ctrl+c
```

Herdr validates all keys before writing any bytes. Read the result through the resolved agent:

```bash
herdr agent get reviewer
herdr agent read reviewer --source recent-unwrapped --lines 120
```

If a wait fails or returns `blocked`, inspect `agent get` and `agent read` before deciding what input to send. Use the pane surface only when raw terminal control is intentional.

## Run an ordinary command in another pane

Create a sibling pane with the same geometry rule, preserve the caller's working directory, and keep user focus unchanged:

```bash
herdr pane split --current --direction right --cwd "$PWD" --no-focus
```

Read the new pane ID from `.result.pane.pane_id`, then run and inspect the command:

```bash
herdr pane run <returned-pane-id> "just test"
herdr pane wait-output <returned-pane-id> --match "test result" --timeout 120000
herdr pane read <returned-pane-id> --source recent-unwrapped --lines 120
```

`pane run` atomically sends command text and Enter. `pane wait-output` searches the selected snapshot immediately, so output that already exists can match. Use `--match <text>` for a literal substring or `--regex <pattern>` for a Rust regular expression. Omitting `--timeout` allows an indefinite wait.

Use the read source that matches the task:

- `visible`: the currently rendered viewport.
- `recent`: recent rendered output, including soft wraps.
- `recent-unwrapped`: recent output with soft wraps joined; prefer it for logs and transcripts.
- `detection`: the plain-text bottom-buffer snapshot used for agent detection.

Use `--format ansi` when colors and terminal styling are evidence. Otherwise use text.

`--lines` asks Herdr for more rows from the pane's available screen and host scrollback. If increasing it does not reveal more of a completed response, the pane is probably running the agent on the terminal's alternate screen. Rows that leave the alternate screen do not enter Herdr's host scrollback, so a larger line count cannot recover them.

After that failed read, ask the agent to write its complete response as Markdown in a temporary directory and reply only with the file path, then read the file directly. Use this only as a fallback; do not request file output in the initial prompt.

## Safety and coordination rules

- Use `--no-focus` for background work unless the user asked to switch context.
- Use `--current`, an explicit pane ID, or a unique agent name. Do not rely on another client's focused pane.
- Parse IDs from JSON responses. Do not derive them from sidebar order or examples.
- Do not close workspaces, tabs, panes, or sessions you did not create unless the user explicitly asked.
- Never run `herdr server stop` from an active session unless the user explicitly intends to stop the server and its pane processes.
- Never kill the main Herdr process. Use named test sessions for experiments that need an isolated server.
- CLI server errors are JSON on stderr with exit status 1. CLI syntax errors exit with status 2.

{"id":"COR-1185","title":"CLI: submit mirror creates through the async mirror-request routes","description":"## Problem

`entire repo mirror create` currently calls `CreateMirror`, waits for a synchronous `CreatedMirror`, and only then polls the mirror status until the initial clone is ready. From Sydney or Mumbai the first of those two waits measured 12–15 seconds under the old 15s gateway wall — and 26.9s (AU) / 28.9s (IN) once that wall was lifted on 2026-08-18 (<pull-request id="4a2e3909-6a1d-472f-9bb5-37b1cd378920" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/review/entire-core-gateway-request-timeout-30s-45s-sized-off-measured-latency-ecc0fc64f07d">entirehq/fleet#4613</pull-request>) — and a caller timeout during it can leave a half-applied placement behind.

[COR-1181](<https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1181>) adds a route that accepts a create and returns immediately: `POST /api/v1/mirror-requests` → **202** with a `Location` pointing at a pollable request resource. This issue moves the CLI onto it.

Both the one-shot command and the wizard already share `createAndAwaitMirror`. Keep that single path — the CLI has been bitten before by the two drifting apart.

## What this is, and is not

It is a route switch, not a response-shape migration. `POST /api/v1/mirrors` is never modified, and the server never sends a 202 to a caller that asked for the old route. There is no header to send, no capability to advertise, and no branching on which response came back. Each invocation selects one route from the local setting.

The CLI keeps both routes during rollout behind a repository-local setting in `.entire/settings.local.json`. Unset or false uses the existing synchronous route; true selects the async route.

There is no capability preflight and no automatic fallback. If the setting selects the async route against a core that does not serve it, fail loudly. A submission-level 404 is not a reliable capability signal because the live route can also return existence-agnostic repository failures.

The setting prevents accidental adoption; it does not prove the backend can complete accepted work. Enable the async path for normal use only after every production region serves the route and its mirror-create consumer is enabled.

## A real simplification

**Resubmitting is safe.** The new route enforces one live request per (provider, owner, repo, cluster); a resubmission returns the *existing* request's 202 and `Location` rather than starting a second placement. So a transport failure before acceptance can simply be retried, rather than needing the careful "did that write land?" reasoning the current code carries.

## Work

**Regenerate the client** for the [COR-1205](<https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1205>) contract.

Give `createAndAwaitMirror` **two explicit phases:**

1. Submit the request and poll it until placement succeeds or terminally fails.
2. With the mirror id from phase one, continue the existing mirror-status poll until the initial clone is ready.

Keep the existing phase-two poll unchanged: `GET /api/v1/mirrors/{mirrorId}` every two seconds with the current bound of 15 consecutive errors (about 30 seconds). After phase one succeeds, the first mirror read can return 404 for roughly five seconds because the SpiceDB `minimize_latency` reverse lookup is not read-after-write consistent. That behavior was accepted on <issue id="6624dff2-dd8d-481e-95a0-abcf39a5d272" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1337/staging-validation-cycle-for-the-async-mirror-create-dispatch-path">COR-1337</issue> and is already covered by the current bound; retry it rather than treating the first 404 as terminal. The manual staging script needed the same bounded retry.

**Carry over the cross-jurisdiction machinery.** The new route returns the same 421 with `home_core_url` for a cluster outside the core's jurisdiction, so the existing cross-jurisdiction round-tripper and token exchange need pointing at the new route, not rebuilding.

Keep `--no-wait` **honest.** It skips waiting for the clone; it does **not** return on a bare acceptance. It still waits until placement is registered and a real mirror id and URL can be printed — which means polling phase one to completion. Worth stating plainly: `--no-wait` does not get dramatically faster, because the work it waits on is the work that was slow. What improves is that the wait is now interruptible and resumable rather than a held-open connection that strands state when it drops.

**Make the progress display legible across both phases.** "Queued", "placing" and "cloning" are different states and a user watching an operation this long deserves to know which one they are in.

Define `--wait-timeout` **over the full placement-plus-clone wait**, unless the upstream contract forces separate deadlines.

---
name: clean-go
description: >
  Focused Go clean-code review and fix workflow for the current diff against origin/main,
  based on modern Go and local Go preferences. By default, fixes only high-confidence,
  unambiguous Required findings in one batch. Use when the user asks for clean Go
  review, Go cleanliness, Go refactoring review, pfleidi:clean-go, or when larger
  Go refactors/code changes need clean Go guidance.
---

# Clean Go Review

Go has generics; do not repeat older guidance that treats lack of generics as a current limitation. Prefer typed APIs over exposing `any`/`interface{}` when they make call sites safer and clearer. Use generics for repeated type-independent algorithms or data structures, not as a replacement for method-based interfaces such as `io.Reader`.

## 1. Determine Diff Against origin/main

Always review the current working tree against `origin/main` directly. Do not use local `main`, `git merge-base`, a PR base branch, or a user-specified alternate base.

```bash
git diff origin/main --stat
git diff origin/main --name-only -- '*.go'
```

Include committed, staged, and unstaged changes. If no Go files changed, report that and stop.

Review only changed Go code plus the surrounding source, tests, interfaces, and call sites needed to confirm or reject a finding. Do not produce broad repo-wide style feedback.

Use permission-friendly reads while investigating. Avoid shell pipelines, command separators, subshells, and output filters for read-only source inspection because they create extra permission prompts and can block background work. Do not run commands like `git show HEAD:path | sed -n '10,40p'`. Use workspace file range reads, `rg` with path limits, path-scoped diffs, or one standalone `git show <rev>:<path>` only when the output is acceptably small.

## 2. Determine Target Go Version

Read the relevant `go.mod` for changed packages and use its `go` directive as the target version. If no Go version is available, do not suggest version-specific modernizations; ask before applying fixes that require a version assumption.

Only recommend modern Go features available in the target version. Do not use newer syntax or APIs just because they are listed here.

## 3. Review Philosophy

- It is OK to find nothing. Do not manufacture style findings.
- Findings must be concrete, source-backed, and limited to changed code.
- Prefer small, local refactor suggestions. Do not propose broad rewrites.
- Respect existing local conventions unless they directly create readability, correctness, or maintainability cost.
- Do not ask for public/shared signature changes unless the cost is justified. Stop before applying such a change.
- Complexity is a lifetime cost. Do not add or endorse interfaces, options structs, generic wrappers, feature flags, config knobs, retry/fallback layers, caches, or concurrency just because a future caller, scale problem, or failure mode might appear.

## 4. Clean Go Checks

Review changed Go code for:

- **Abstraction level** - functions/methods should stay at one level of abstraction; high-level code should orchestrate meaningful helpers instead of embedding low-level IO, parsing, protocol, or data-structure details.
- **Composable flow** - avoid pass-through helper chains that only thread parameters into the next helper. Do not add methods whose only behavior is calling another method on the same receiver with the same inputs plus a constant/default argument; prefer the direct call unless an external interface, compatibility boundary, validation, instrumentation, or other real responsibility requires the wrapper. When a new parameter is part of the current design, update the callers instead of adding defaulting receiver methods to preserve the old call shape. Prefer meaningful intermediate values where they clarify the flow.
- **Function purpose and size** - functions should do one cohesive job, avoid indentation-heavy logic, and use early returns when they make the main path easier to read. Treat about 20 lines as a review smell, not a hard limit. Do not split a function solely to hit a line count; helper extraction must create a meaningful, composable abstraction.
- **Function naming** - broader-scope functions can have broader names; smaller/lower-level helpers should have more specific names that stand alone at their call sites.
- **Variable naming and scope** - declare values close to use; keep mutable scope narrow; short names are fine only when the local context makes them obvious.
- **Function signatures** - prefer small signatures. Treat more than 3-4 inputs, unclear boolean arguments, and repeated primitive groups as review smells. Consider an options struct only when current call sites already have enough optional or repeated fields that grouping them improves call-site clarity; do not create one for a single weak optional field, a single caller, or hypothetical future parameters.
- **Return values** - prefer concrete return types when practical. Avoid ambiguous `(result, bool)` returns except clear comma-ok/presence signals such as `ok`, `found`, or `exists`. Use named result parameters only when they clarify documentation or deferred mutation; avoid naked returns in non-trivial functions.
- **Errors** - do not discard errors; avoid panic for ordinary errors; use lowercase error strings without trailing punctuation. Avoid magic-string error checks; prefer sentinel errors, typed errors, or narrow predicate helpers when callers need to branch. Use `errors.Is` for categories and sentinels; use `errors.As` only when the caller needs the concrete typed error value. Use `%w` only when exposing the wrapped error is part of the API; otherwise use `%v`, return the error directly, or add context without wrapping. Avoid generic wrapper prefixes that do not improve diagnosis, especially when the lower-level error already names the resource and reason. When changed code handles `err != nil` with a retry, fallback, `continue`, default value, or generic message, check whether distinct error classes are being collapsed.
- **Contexts and goroutines** - pass `context.Context` as the first parameter after the receiver, do not store it in structs, and do not define custom context interfaces. New goroutines should have clear cancellation, ownership, and exit behavior.
- **Pointers and mutation** - use pointers deliberately; minimize pointer-driven mutation, nil risk, and exposed mutable state. Do not pass pointers merely to avoid small copies, and do not copy values containing synchronization primitives or types whose methods imply pointer ownership.
- **Test seams and mutable globals** - do not introduce mutable function variables, package-wide settings, exported reset hooks, or other production state solely so tests can swap dependencies. Prefer dependency injection through existing construction paths or small typed interfaces; if that would distort the production design, use a higher-scope integration test.
- **Interfaces** - keep interfaces small; accept interfaces where useful and return concrete types where practical. Avoid embedded interfaces that create nil-panic or partial-implementation traps.
- **any/interface{}** - do not expose `any`/`interface{}` when a typed API or generic function/type would make misuse harder. Keep unavoidable dynamic typing behind a typed wrapper.
- **Naming and packages** - follow Go initialism casing such as `ID` and `URL`; prefer short, descriptive package names and avoid vague packages like `util`, `common`, or `types` unless the local codebase already uses them intentionally.
- **Slices and JSON** - distinguish nil and empty slices when API or JSON output depends on it; otherwise prefer the simpler representation used locally.
- **Comments** - comments default to zero. Keep only linter-required public API docs or a concise non-obvious why: a hidden current constraint, workaround for a specific bug, surprising behavior, or external requirement. Flag explanatory blocks above ordinary code; prefer clearer names, helpers, or simpler flow.
- **Tests and refactors** - refactors that affect behavior or risk should include focused tests in the same diff. Check that tests exercise meaningful behavior at the right scope: unit tests for focused logic with natural dependencies, integration tests for real wiring/config/filesystems/databases/framework behavior, and end-to-end or smoke tests only for critical full-system flows. Do not treat fast unit tests as weak merely because they skip wiring that integration/e2e tests own; preserve useful unit tests and add a narrow integration/e2e test only for a real uncovered boundary. For error-handling changes, require focused tests for observable classification with `errors.Is`/`errors.As`, preserved wrapping where callers depend on it, and user-facing text when boundary output changes.
- **Test helper readability** - use `skills/pfleidi/testing/SKILL.md` as the source of truth. Helpers should make tests more readable, not merely remove a few lines of duplication. In Go, prefer table-driven tests or subtests when repeated cases share logic; keep important inputs, expected values, and assertions visible at the call site; call `t.Helper()` in helpers that fail tests.

## 5. Modern Go Checks

Apply these checks only when supported by the target Go version:

---
name: testing
description: >
  Local testing strategy and review guidance for meaningful tests, choosing unit vs integration vs end-to-end scope,
  avoiding production-only test seams and over-mocking, and keeping test helpers readable, especially in Go.
  Use when writing, changing, or reviewing tests; adding mocks or test helpers; deciding test scope; or when user mentions pfleidi:testing.
---

# Testing Guidance

## Core Principle

Tests should make changed behavior trustworthy without distorting production code. Prefer behavior and contracts over implementation details. Use the smallest scope that gives real confidence.

## Never Use Real Customer Data

**NEVER put real customer data in test cases.** No production records, real PII, real emails, real account/customer IDs, or scrubbed copies of live data — "anonymized" or "scrubbed" production data is still forbidden. Fabricate synthetic fixtures that exercise the same shape and edge cases. When reviewing, reject any test carrying real customer data outright.

## Choose Test Scope

- **Unit tests** - pure logic, parsing, validation, small components, and behavior with explicit dependencies that can be supplied naturally.
- **Integration tests** - real wiring, filesystem, config, databases, process boundaries, generated code, framework behavior, or cases where unit isolation would require awkward mocks or production-only seams.
- **End-to-end / smoke tests** - critical user or system flows across process or service boundaries. Keep these few, stable, and high value.

Cover changed behavior, important edge cases, and error paths. Do not chase line coverage with brittle tests that only exercise private structure.

## Preserve Test Layers

Unit, integration, and end-to-end suites are complementary layers with different costs. A fast unit suite may intentionally skip real wiring, config, databases, filesystems, generated code, or framework behavior when another suite owns that boundary. That is not incomplete unit testing; it is a useful split of responsibilities.

Before changing test scope, identify the missing confidence:

- If the gap is pure logic, parsing, validation, or small behavior with natural dependencies, add or adjust a unit test.
- If the gap is real wiring, config loading, filesystem/database behavior, generated code, process boundaries, or framework behavior, first check existing integration/e2e coverage. If coverage is missing, add a narrow integration/e2e test at that boundary.
- Preserve useful fast unit tests. Do not rewrite broad unit test suites into integration tests just to cover wiring. Convert a unit test only when its stated subject is wrong and an additive test at the right layer would not cover the gap.

## Avoid Production Test Seams

Do not add production code that exists only to make tests easier:

- Mutable function variables swapped in tests.
- Mutable package-wide settings changed by tests.
- Exported `Reset`, `Set`, or hook functions only used by tests.
- Global clocks, filesystems, HTTP clients, env readers, or command runners added only for unit tests.

If a test needs these, prefer dependency injection through existing construction paths, small typed interfaces around external effects, or a higher-scope integration test.

## Test Helpers

Helpers are useful when they make the test shorter and easier to understand. They are harmful when they hide the behavior being tested.

Use a helper when:

- It removes noisy setup or cleanup that is not the point of the test.
- Its name is domain-specific and explains what the caller gets.
- The test remains understandable without opening the helper.
- It preserves the important inputs, expected values, and assertions at the call site.

Inline the code instead when:

- The helper saves only a few lines but hides the arrange/act/assert flow.
- The reviewer must inspect the helper to know what behavior is asserted.
- The helper takes booleans, loose maps, or option bags that obscure intent.
- The helper embeds important defaults, expected values, or failure conditions.
- The helper is generic test plumbing with no domain meaning.

Prefer local helpers in the test file until reuse is clear. Moving helpers to shared test utilities raises the readability bar because future readers lose locality.

## Go-Specific Helper Rules

- Prefer table-driven tests or `t.Run` subtests when repeated cases share the same logic. Each table row should be a complete scenario with inputs, expected outputs, and a clear name.
- Keep expected values in the table row or test body. Do not hide them in helper defaults.
- Use `t.Run` names to identify cases, then keep failure messages focused on `got` vs `want`.
- If a helper can fail the test, accept `testing.TB` or `*testing.T` and call `t.Helper()` first so failures point to the caller.
- Use `t.Cleanup`, `t.TempDir`, and `t.Setenv` for resource setup when appropriate. Remember that process-wide changes such as environment or current-directory changes are not safe for parallel tests unless the testing API says so.
- Return concrete values from builders. Avoid global shared fixtures and mutable package state.

# Upstream Core API fixes

This client carries workarounds for bugs/gaps in the control-plane
OpenAPI document and its surface. Each item below should be fixed at the
source (the control-plane service's spec generation / route design);
doing so lets us delete the corresponding workaround here and regenerate
a cleaner client. This file is the running checklist.

When an item is fixed upstream, remove its workaround (cited by file) and
delete the entry.

## 1. Operations enumerate every error status with no shared `default`

**Symptom:** each operation declares its real success code (good — 201
for creates, 200 for reads, 204 for deletes) but then lists every error
status separately (`400`, `401`, `403`, `422`, `500`, …) with no
`default` response. ogen turns that into a per-operation sum-type result,
forcing a type switch at every call site instead of the ergonomic
`(*T, error)`.

**Fix upstream:** emit a single `default` error response (every error
already references the same `ErrorModel`, so a `default` is lossless).
ogen then generates "convenient errors" — `(*T, error)` with non-2xx as a
typed `*ErrorModelStatusCode` — straight from the spec.

**Workaround:** `spec/normalize.go` (`foldErrorResponses`) folds each
operation's explicit 4xx/5xx into one `default`, keeping the real success
code untouched. This is the one transform that is a deliberate
ergonomics choice rather than a pure bug workaround; a shared `default`
upstream retires it.

## 2. Display-only read enums hard-fail on unknown values

**Symptom:** read-model string fields the CLI only displays (`Repo.state`,
`Repo.visibility`, `Repo.objectFormat`) are declared as `enum`. ogen turns
each into a named type with a strict `Validate()` that the response decoder
calls unconditionally, so the day the server adds a new value (a new repo
lifecycle state, say) the whole `repo list` / repo-get request fails to
decode — even though the client never branches on the value.

**Fix upstream:** model client-display fields that may grow new values as
plain strings (drop `enum`), or have ogen treat them as open enums. Enums
the *client sends* (request bodies like `SetRepoVisibilityInputBody`) should
stay strict.

**Workaround:** `spec/normalize.go` (`loosenReadModelEnums`, allowlist
`readModelEnumFields`) deletes the `enum` constraint from those response
read-model fields, so ogen emits plain strings with no `Validate()` and
unknown values pass through for display. Only response read models are
loosened; request-body enums stay strict. Locked in by
`TestListProjectRepos_UnknownEnumValuesPassThrough` in `client_test.go`.
Retire the allowlist entries as upstream loosens the corresponding fields.

<!-- Resolved upstream and removed:
  - Nullable arrays (`"type": ["array","null"]`) — entiredb now emits
    non-nullable arrays (`"type": "array"`, absent ⇒ `[]`), so the
    `collapseTypeUnions` transform is gone.
  - by-mirror lookup vs mirrorId delete — entiredb ENT-741 replaced the
    two-call lookup→delete with a single delete-by-coords route
    (`DELETE /mirrors?provider&owner&repo&clusterHost`); `mirror remove`
    now calls it directly and surfaces the new 404/403/503 contract. -->

+func TestCreateAndAwaitMirror_AsyncCancellation(t *testing.T) {
+	previousInterval := mirrorPollInterval
+	mirrorPollInterval = time.Millisecond
+	t.Cleanup(func() { mirrorPollInterval = previousInterval })
+
+	for _, phase := range []string{"placement", "clone"} {
+		t.Run(phase, func(t *testing.T) {
+			ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(t.Context())
+			pollStarted := make(chan struct{})
+			srv := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
+				switch {
+				case r.URL.Path == mirrorRequestsAPIPath:
+					w.Header().Set("Location", mirrorRequestPath())
+					if phase == "clone" {
+						writeSuccessfulMirrorRequestWithStatus(t, w, http.StatusAccepted)
+					} else {
+						w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
+						w.WriteHeader(http.StatusAccepted)
+						writeMirrorRequestBody(t, w, coreapi.MirrorRequest{RequestId: testMirrorRequestID, Status: coreapi.MirrorRequestStatusPending})
+					}
+				case phase == "placement" && r.URL.Path == mirrorRequestPath():
+					close(pollStarted)
+					<-r.Context().Done()
+				case phase == "clone" && strings.HasPrefix(r.URL.Path, "/api/v1/mirrors/"):
+					close(pollStarted)
+					<-r.Context().Done()
+				default:
+					t.Errorf("unexpected request %s %s", r.Method, r.URL.Path)
+				}
+			}))
+			t.Cleanup(srv.Close)
+			client, err := coreapi.NewWithBearer(srv.URL, "token")
+			require.NoError(t, err)
+
+			result := make(chan error, 1)
+			go func() {
+				_, err := createAndAwaitMirror(ctx, client, "owner", "repo", "cluster", mirrorCreateOptions{
+					async: true, timeout: time.Second,
+				})
+				result <- err
+			}()
+			<-pollStarted
+			cancel()
+			err = <-result
+			var silent *SilentError
+			require.ErrorAs(t, err, &silent)
+		})
+	}
+}
+
+func mirrorRequestPath() string {
+	return mirrorRequestsAPIPath + "/" + testMirrorRequestID.String()
+}
+
+func writeAcceptedMirrorRequest(t *testing.T, w http.ResponseWriter, status coreapi.MirrorRequestStatus) {
+	t.Helper()
+	w.Header().Set("Location", mirrorRequestPath())
+	writeJSONResponse(t, w, http.StatusAccepted, coreapi.MirrorRequest{RequestId: testMirrorRequestID, Status: status})
+}
+
+func writeSuccessfulMirrorRequest(t *testing.T, w http.ResponseWriter) {
+	t.Helper()
+	writeSuccessfulMirrorRequestWithStatus(t, w, http.StatusOK)
+}
+
+func writeSuccessfulMirrorRequestWithStatus(t *testing.T, w http.ResponseWriter, status int) {
+	t.Helper()
+	request := coreapi.MirrorRequest{RequestId: testMirrorRequestID, Status: coreapi.MirrorRequestStatusSucceeded}
+	request.Result = coreapi.NewOptMirrorRequestResult(coreapi.MirrorRequestResult{
+		MirrorId: "mirror-1", MirrorUrl: "entire://cluster/gh/owner/repo", PublicUrl: "https://cluster/gh/owner/repo",
+	})
+	writeJSONResponse(t, w, status, request)
+}
+
+func writeMirrorRequest(t *testing.T, w http.ResponseWriter, request coreapi.MirrorRequest) {
+	t.Helper()
+	writeJSONResponse(t, w, http.StatusOK, request)
+}
+
+func writeJSONResponse(t *testing.T, w http.ResponseWriter, status int, value any) {
+	t.Helper()
+	w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
+	w.WriteHeader(status)
+	writeMirrorRequestBody(t, w, value)
+}
+
+func writeMirrorRequestBody(t *testing.T, w http.ResponseWriter, value any) {
+	t.Helper()
+	if err := printJSON(w, value); err != nil {
+		t.Errorf("encode response: %v", err)
+	}
+}
+
+func writeCoreProblem(t *testing.T, w http.ResponseWriter, status int, detail string) {
+	t.Helper()
+	w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/problem+json")
+	w.WriteHeader(status)
+	if _, err := w.Write([]byte(`{"title":"request failed","detail":"` + detail + `","status":` + http.StatusText(status) + `}`)); err != nil {
+		t.Errorf("write problem response: %v", err)
+	}
+}
*** End Patch";

<skills_instructions>
## Skills
A skill is a set of local instructions to follow that is stored in a `SKILL.md` file. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and a short path that can be expanded into an absolute path using the skill roots table.
### Skill roots
- `r0` = `/Users/pfleidi/.agents/skills`
- `r1` = `/Users/pfleidi/.codex/skills/.system`
- `r2` = `/Users/pfleidi/.codex/plugins/cache/openai-curated-remote`
### Available skills
- skill-creator: Create or update a Codex skill with appropriately scoped instructions and any needed supporting resources. (file: r1/skill-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-installer: Install Codex skills into $CODEX_HOME/skills from a curated list or a GitHub repo path. Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos). (file: r1/skill-installer/SKILL.md)
- context7-mcp: This skill should be used when the user asks about libraries, frameworks, API references, or needs code examples. Activates for setup questions, code generation involving libraries, or mentions of specific frameworks like React, Vue, Next.js, Prisma, Supabase, etc. (file: r0/context7-mcp/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:clean-go: Focused Go clean-code review and fix workflow for the current diff against origin/main, based on modern Go and local Go preferences. By default, fixes only high-confidence, unambiguous Required findings in one batch. Use when the user asks for clean Go review, Go cleanliness, Go refactoring review, pfleidi:clean-go, or when larger Go refactors/code changes need clean Go guidance. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/clean-go/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:daily-status: Use when the user asks for a daily Slack status, standup update, work recap, report since a previous update, or a summary of recent Linear, authored GitHub PR, Entire trail, and work-related Slack activity. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/daily-status/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:de-slop: Use when the user asks to de-slop, simplify code, remove cruft, reduce over-abstraction, clean up weak tests, simplify a current branch or named code area, or explicitly invokes pfleidi:de-slop. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/de-slop/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:explain-diff: Use when the user asks for a rich explanation, teaching-style walkthrough, or shareable writeup of a code change, diff, branch, commit, or PR — e.g. "explain this diff", "help me understand this PR", "make an explainer for this change" — or invokes /explain-diff. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/explain-diff/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:feedback: Use when the user asks to fix, address, explain, triage, respond to, dismiss, resolve, publish, or watch remote review feedback for the current branch; mentions Bugbot, Copilot, GitHub PR comments, or Entire trail findings; or invokes /feedback or pfleidi:feedback. Also collects read-only local findings alongside remote intake. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/feedback/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:guided-research: Use when the user asks for guided research, deep research, codebase understanding, a coworker-readable research artifact, answers to annotated research docs, or live watching of a Markdown research artifact. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/guided-research/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:investigate-alert: Use when the user provides a Datadog monitor URL/ID, Datadog event URL, pasted alert text, incident, or monitor name and asks whether it is noise, why it fired, how to investigate it, how to tune it, or invokes /investigate-alert. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/investigate-alert/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:pr: Use when the user wants to create, open, or make a GitHub pull request for the current branch, asks to prepare the branch for PR creation, provides an optional PR target base branch, or invokes /pr. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/pr/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:project-shape: Use when the user wants to investigate, define, or substantially restructure a multi-issue engineering project; turn a parent issue into thin vertical slices; identify spikes, dependencies, parallel work, risks, or completion criteria; or invokes project-shape. Do not use for a routine morning project reconciliation when project-update applies. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/project-shape/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:project-update: Use for a fast morning or recurring update of an existing multi-issue engineering project: reconcile material issue and pull-request changes, findings, blockers, flags, rollout or validation state; propose tracker corrections; record a concise parent update; and prioritize the next five meaningful steps. Do not use for initial project design or substantial restructuring when project-shape applies. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/project-update/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:remote-review: Use when the user asks for local feedback on a GitHub PR or Entire trail, provides a PR/trail URL or number, asks to review an Entire trail, asks for PR/trail feedback without fixing it, or explicitly invokes pfleidi:remote-review. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/remote-review/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:review: Use when the user asks to review the current branch, review a local diff, audit code changes before merge, run a code review or full review, or invokes /review. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/review/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:task-align: Align a single Linear or GitHub task before execution by verifying the problem, separating facts from proposals, settling material decisions, and defining development and post-deploy validation. Use when issue-derived work has unclear evidence, scope, behavior, risk, or validation, or when task-implement requests alignment. Skip clear, small tasks with no material decisions. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/task-align/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:task-implement: Start and implement one well-scoped Linear or GitHub task: align it when needed, update native tracker state, run no-code work in a coordinator-workspace tab, or create an Entire worktree and focused implementation session when repository changes are required. Use Herdr when active; otherwise use the invoking session. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/task-implement/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:task-validate: Perform isolated final validation of one implemented Linear or GitHub task against its live exit criteria and the full approved commit range. Use a temporary Entire worktree and, when already under Herdr, a dedicated validation tab and agent that can report code failures to the implementation agent. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/task-validate/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:testing: Local testing strategy and review guidance for meaningful tests, choosing unit vs integration vs end-to-end scope, avoiding production-only test seams and over-mocking, and keeping test helpers readable, especially in Go. Use when writing, changing, or reviewing tests; adding mocks or test helpers; deciding test scope; or when user mentions pfleidi:testing. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/testing/SKILL.md)
- plugin-management:plugin-management: Discover and suggest relevant plugins, inspect app permissions and dependencies, and manage plugin connections or removal. Use when the user asks about plugins or when a task would materially benefit from an external app, account, service, or data source that available tools cannot access. (file: r2/plugin-management/0.1.0/skills/plugin-management/SKILL.md)
- search: Use when the user wants to find prior work, checkpoints, or agent conversations by topic, repo, branch, author, or recent time window, or to search code content across repositories (file: r0/search/SKILL.md)
- using-entire: Use when codebase exploration or explanation would benefit from historical implementation intent recorded in Entire checkpoints. Combines current source with checkpoint evidence without treating unavailable history as a blocker. (file: r0/using-entire/SKILL.md)
</skills_instructions>

<permissions instructions>
Filesystem sandboxing defines which files can be read or written. `sandbox_mode` is `workspace-write`: The sandbox permits reading files, and editing files in `cwd` and `writable_roots`. Editing files in other directories requires approval. Network access is restricted.
# Escalation Requests

Commands are run outside the sandbox if they are approved by the user, or match an existing rule that allows it to run unrestricted. The command string is split into independent command segments at shell control operators, including but not limited to:

- Pipes: |
- Logical operators: &&, ||
- Command separators: ;
- Subshell boundaries: (...), $(...)

Each resulting segment is evaluated independently for sandbox restrictions and approval requirements.

Example:

git pull | tee output.txt

This is treated as two command segments:

["git", "pull"]

["tee", "output.txt"]

Commands that use more advanced shell features like redirection (>, >>, <), substitutions ($(...), ...), environment variables (FOO=bar), or wildcard patterns (*, ?) will not be evaluated against rules, to limit the scope of what an approved rule allows.

## How to request escalation

IMPORTANT: To request approval to execute a command that will require escalated privileges:

- Provide the `sandbox_permissions` parameter with the value `"require_escalated"`
- Include a short question asking the user if they want to allow the action in `justification` parameter. e.g. "Do you want to download and install dependencies for this project?"
- Optionally suggest a `prefix_rule` - this will be shown to the user with an option to persist the rule approval for future sessions.

If you run a command that is important to solving the user's query, but it fails because of sandboxing or with a likely sandbox-related network error (for example DNS/host resolution, registry/index access, or dependency download failure), rerun the command with "require_escalated". ALWAYS proceed to use the `justification` parameter - do not message the user before requesting approval for the command.

## When to request escalation

While commands are running inside the sandbox, here are some scenarios that will require escalation outside the sandbox:

- You need to run a command that writes to a directory that requires it (e.g. running tests that write to /var)
- You need to run a GUI app (e.g., open/xdg-open/osascript) to open browsers or files.
- If you run a command that is important to solving the user's query, but it fails because of sandboxing or with a likely sandbox-related network error (for example DNS/host resolution, registry/index access, or dependency download failure), rerun the command with `require_escalated`. ALWAYS proceed to use the `sandbox_permissions` and `justification` parameters. do not message the user before requesting approval for the command.
- You are about to take a potentially destructive action such as an `rm` or `git reset` that the user did not explicitly ask for.
- Be judicious with escalating, but if completing the user's request requires it, you should do so - don't try and circumvent approvals by using other tools.

## prefix_rule guidance

When choosing a `prefix_rule`, request one that will allow you to fulfill similar requests from the user in the future without re-requesting escalation. It should be categorical and reasonably scoped to similar capabilities. You should rarely pass the entire command into `prefix_rule`.

### Banned prefix_rules 
Avoid requesting overly broad prefixes that the user would be ill-advised to approve. For example, do not request ["python3"], ["python", "-"], or other similar prefixes that would allow arbitrary scripting.
NEVER provide a prefix_rule argument for destructive commands like rm.
NEVER provide a prefix_rule if your command uses a heredoc or herestring. 

### Examples
Good examples of prefixes:
- ["npm", "run", "dev"]
- ["gh", "pr", "check"]
- ["cargo", "test"]


## Approved command prefixes
The following prefix rules have already been approved: - ["ps"]
- ["gofmt"]
- ["gh", "api"]
- ["go", "vet"]
- ["git", "log"]
- ["go", "test"]

You are now in Default mode. Any previous instructions for other modes (e.g. Plan mode) are no longer active.

Your active mode changes only when new developer instructions with a different `<collaboration_mode>...</collaboration_mode>` change it; user requests or tool descriptions do not change mode by themselves. Known mode names are Default and Plan.
