## Skills
A skill is a set of local instructions to follow that is stored in a `SKILL.md` file. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and a short path that can be expanded into an absolute path using the skill roots table.
### Skill roots
- `r0` = `/Users/pfleidi/.agents/skills`
- `r1` = `/Users/pfleidi/.codex/skills/.system`
- `r2` = `/Users/pfleidi/.codex/plugins/cache/openai-curated-remote`
### Available skills
- skill-creator: Create or update a Codex skill with appropriately scoped instructions and any needed supporting resources. (file: r1/skill-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-installer: Install Codex skills into $CODEX_HOME/skills from a curated list or a GitHub repo path. Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos). (file: r1/skill-installer/SKILL.md)
- context7-mcp: This skill should be used when the user asks about libraries, frameworks, API references, or needs code examples. Activates for setup questions, code generation involving libraries, or mentions of specific frameworks like React, Vue, Next.js, Prisma, Supabase, etc. (file: r0/context7-mcp/SKILL.md)
- pfleidi:clean-go: Focused Go clean-code review and fix workflow for the current diff against origin/main, based on modern Go and local Go preferences. By default, fixes only high-confidence, unambiguous Required findings in one batch. Use when the user asks for clean Go review, Go cleanliness, Go refactoring review, pfleidi:clean-go, or when larger Go refactors/code changes need clean Go guidance. (file: r0/pfleidi/skills/clean-go/SKILL.md)

---
name: explain-diff
description: >
  Use when the user asks for a rich explanation, teaching-style walkthrough,
  or shareable writeup of a code change, diff, branch, commit, or PR — e.g.
  "explain this diff", "help me understand this PR", "make an explainer for
  this change" — or invokes /explain-diff.
---

# Explain Diff

Produce a rich, interactive HTML explanation of a code change, written for a
reader who did not make the change.

## 1. Determine the Change

- If the user names a PR, commit, range, or files, explain exactly that.
- Otherwise default to the current branch: diff the working tree against the
  merge base with `origin/main`, and read `git log origin/main..HEAD` for
  intent.
- Broadly explore the surrounding code, not just the diff — the Background
  section must rest on how the existing system actually works.

## 2. Recover Intent and Provenance

Treat Entire provenance as a primary source, alongside the diff and current
code. Use it early and repeatedly to recover the decisions, constraints,
feedback, and alternatives behind the change instead of guessing from commit
messages.

1. Run `entire status`. If Entire is unavailable or the repository has no
   history, continue with Git and source evidence; do not enable or configure
   it as part of this read-only workflow.
2. Identify the relevant commits from the change boundary. Inspect each commit
   with `entire checkpoint explain --commit <sha> --json --no-pager`. When its
   metadata indicates relevant intent, feedback, or decisions, read the
   targeted transcript with
   `entire checkpoint explain --commit <sha> --full --no-pager`.
3. Search beyond directly attached checkpoints with several focused queries:

   ```bash
   entire search "<issue ID, symbol, feature, or decision phrase>" --compact --limit 10
   ```

   Search related terminology, rejected approaches, review feedback, and
   cross-cutting constraints. Add `--all-repos` when the change depends on work
   in another repository. Drill into useful hits with:

   ```bash
   entire checkpoint explain <checkpoint-id> --full --no-pager
   entire checkpoint explain <checkpoint-id> --repo <owner/name> --full --no-pager
   ```

4. Build a small provenance map before drafting: current code behavior, diff,
   recorded intent, decisions and alternatives, primary-source URLs, and any
   remaining inference. Include links for the change itself and for named
   issues, design documents, or review threads when available. Use
   checkpoint-backed facts throughout Background, Intuition, and Code; label
   code-only inference as inference. Synthesize the evidence rather than
   pasting transcripts.

If a sandboxed Entire command reports a suspicious authentication, keychain,
or missing-session failure, retry the exact command in the host context once
before treating provenance as unavailable.

## 3. Content

One long page with section headers and a table of contents. No tabs for the
top-level structure. Four sections:

- **Background**: the existing system relevant to this change. Start with a
  deep background for beginners (note it can be skipped by readers who know
  the system), then the narrow background directly relevant to the change.
- **Intuition**: the core idea of the change — essence, not full detail.
  Concrete examples with toy data. Figures and diagrams used liberally.
- **Code**: a high-level walkthrough of the changes, grouped and ordered so
  the reader can follow the shape of the change rather than the file order.
- **Quiz**: five interactive multiple-choice questions, medium difficulty —
  answerable only by someone who understood the substance, but no gotchas.
  Clicking an answer reveals whether it was correct plus short feedback.

Write with the clarity and flow of Martin Kleppmann: engaging, classic style,
smooth transitions between sections.

Build one causal thread through the page. Order topics by what the reader needs
to understand next, not by file, component, or discovery order. Before
introducing a new subsystem or mechanism, connect it to the problem already in
view: state what unanswered question it resolves, why it matters to this
change, and how the preceding behavior reaches it. A heading is not a
transition. Each subsection should leave the reader with either a conclusion
or a question that makes the next subsection feel necessary.

The explanation must stand on its own, while making it easy to inspect primary
sources:

- Link the PR, commit, or comparison being explained and link each named issue,
  design document, or review thread at its first meaningful mention. Label PR
  and issue links as `ID (title)`.
- Add nearby source links for consequential behavior, constraints, decisions,
  and tradeoffs. Prefer stable GitHub permalinks to relevant source or tests
  and direct issue or design-document links over generic repository pages.
- Keep links selective: usually one to three useful primary sources per
  substantive section. Do not link every symbol or turn the prose into a
  citation list. Readers who never follow a link should still understand the
  argument.
- Never invent a URL. If a primary source is unavailable or cannot be linked,
  say what evidence supports the claim and leave it unlinked.

Before styling the page, reread the headings plus the first and last paragraph
of every subsection as one outline. Rewrite any boundary where the new topic's
connection to the preceding problem is not explicit. Then scan named PR,
commit, issue, and design-document references and confirm that each available
primary source is linked at its first meaningful mention.

## 4. Diagrams and Formatting

- Pick a small number of diagram families and reuse them throughout to explain
  the different cases. Useful families: a very simplified sketch of the UI the
  user sees (for UI changes), and a system diagram showing data flow between
  components — always with example data in it.
- Never use ASCII diagrams. Build diagrams from simple styled HTML; use HTML
  lists for lists of things.
- Use `<pre>` for code blocks. A custom-styled div must set
  `white-space: pre-wrap` (or `pre`), or the browser collapses all newlines
  into one line. Before saving, scan every code block in the HTML source and
  confirm its CSS includes one of those values.
- Use callouts for key concepts, definitions, and important edge cases.
- Basic responsive styling so the page reads well on a phone.

## 5. Output File

A single self-contained HTML file: all CSS and JavaScript inline, with no
external runtime dependencies. Outbound source links are allowed; opening the
page itself must not fetch scripts, styles, fonts, images, or other assets.
Start the file with a `<title>` and omit the `<!DOCTYPE>`, `<html>`, `<head>`,
and `<body>` wrappers — browsers render the file fine locally, and the same
file then publishes cleanly as a Claude artifact. Give the body an explicit
background color.

The file is ephemeral — save it to `/tmp`, outside the repo so it stays out of
version control, date-prefixed so files sort by time:

```bash
# /tmp/$(date +%Y-%m-%d)-explanation-<slug>.html
```

Report the file path and offer to open it (`open <path>` on macOS).

## 6. Optional: Publish as Claude Artifact

Only in Claude Code, and only when the user asks for an artifact or a
shareable link: publish the same file with the Artifact tool. Load the
`artifact-design` skill before writing the HTML when publishing is requested
up front. Use a short noun-phrase `<title>`, keep the favicon stable across
redeploys, and redeploy with the same file path to update. Artifacts start
private. In other runtimes, skip this section.

## Tracker References

In human-facing prose, render every issue or pull request as `ID (title)` and
link the whole label when a URL exists. Never show a bare tracker ID or issue/PR
URL. Raw IDs remain valid in commands, API fields, branches, paths, and internal
identifiers.

---
name: explain-diff
description: >
  Use when the user asks for a rich explanation, teaching-style walkthrough,
  or shareable writeup of a code change, diff, branch, commit, or PR — e.g.
  "explain this diff", "help me understand this PR", "make an explainer for
  this change" — or invokes /explain-diff.
---

# Explain Diff

Produce a rich, interactive HTML explanation of a code change, written for a
reader who did not make the change.

## 1. Determine the Change

- If the user names a PR, commit, range, or files, explain exactly that.
- Otherwise default to the current branch: diff the working tree against the
  merge base with `origin/main`, and read `git log origin/main..HEAD` for
  intent.
- Broadly explore the surrounding code, not just the diff — the Background
  section must rest on how the existing system actually works.

## 2. Recover Intent and Provenance

Treat Entire provenance as a primary source, alongside the diff and current
code. Use it early and repeatedly to recover the decisions, constraints,
feedback, and alternatives behind the change instead of guessing from commit
messages.

1. Run `entire status`. If Entire is unavailable or the repository has no
   history, continue with Git and source evidence; do not enable or configure
   it as part of this read-only workflow.
2. Identify the relevant commits from the change boundary. Inspect each commit
   with `entire checkpoint explain --commit <sha> --json --no-pager`. When its
   metadata indicates relevant intent, feedback, or decisions, read the
   targeted transcript with
   `entire checkpoint explain --commit <sha> --full --no-pager`.
3. Search beyond directly attached checkpoints with several focused queries:

   ```bash
   entire search "<issue ID, symbol, feature, or decision phrase>" --compact --limit 10
   ```

   Search related terminology, rejected approaches, review feedback, and
   cross-cutting constraints. Add `--all-repos` when the change depends on work
   in another repository. Drill into useful hits with:

   ```bash
   entire checkpoint explain <checkpoint-id> --full --no-pager
   entire checkpoint explain <checkpoint-id> --repo <owner/name> --full --no-pager
   ```

4. Build a small provenance map before drafting: current code behavior, diff,
   recorded intent, decisions and alternatives, primary-source URLs, and any
   remaining inference. Include links for the change itself and for named
   issues, design documents, or review threads when available. Use
   checkpoint-backed facts throughout Background, Intuition, and Code; label
   code-only inference as inference. Synthesize the evidence rather than
   pasting transcripts.

If a sandboxed Entire command reports a suspicious authentication, keychain,
or missing-session failure, retry the exact command in the host context once
before treating provenance as unavailable.

## 3. Content

One long page with section headers and a table of contents. No tabs for the
top-level structure. Four sections:

- **Background**: the existing system relevant to this change. Start with a
  deep background for beginners (note it can be skipped by readers who know
  the system), then the narrow background directly relevant to the change.
- **Intuition**: the core idea of the change — essence, not full detail.
  Concrete examples with toy data. Figures and diagrams used liberally.
- **Code**: a high-level walkthrough of the changes, grouped and ordered so
  the reader can follow the shape of the change rather than the file order.
- **Quiz**: five interactive multiple-choice questions, medium difficulty —
  answerable only by someone who understood the substance, but no gotchas.
  Clicking an answer reveals whether it was correct plus short feedback.

Write with the clarity and flow of Martin Kleppmann: engaging, classic style,
smooth transitions between sections.

Build one causal thread through the page. Order topics by what the reader needs
to understand next, not by file, component, or discovery order. Before
introducing a new subsystem or mechanism, connect it to the problem already in
view: state what unanswered question it resolves, why it matters to this
change, and how the preceding behavior reaches it. A heading is not a
transition. Each subsection should leave the reader with either a conclusion
or a question that makes the next subsection feel necessary.

The explanation must stand on its own, while making it easy to inspect primary
sources:

- Link the PR, commit, or comparison being explained and link each named issue,
  design document, or review thread at its first meaningful mention. Label PR
  and issue links as `ID (title)`.
- Add nearby source links for consequential behavior, constraints, decisions,
  and tradeoffs. Prefer stable GitHub permalinks to relevant source or tests
  and direct issue or design-document links over generic repository pages.
- Keep links selective: usually one to three useful primary sources per
  substantive section. Do not link every symbol or turn the prose into a
  citation list. Readers who never follow a link should still understand the
  argument.
- Never invent a URL. If a primary source is unavailable or cannot be linked,
  say what evidence supports the claim and leave it unlinked.

Before styling the page, reread the headings plus the first and last paragraph
of every subsection as one outline. Rewrite any boundary where the new topic's
connection to the preceding problem is not explicit. Then scan named PR,
commit, issue, and design-document references and confirm that each available
primary source is linked at its first meaningful mention.

## 4. Diagrams and Formatting

- Pick a small number of diagram families and reuse them throughout to explain
  the different cases. Useful families: a very simplified sketch of the UI the
  user sees (for UI changes), and a system diagram showing data flow between
  components — always with example data in it.
- Never use ASCII diagrams. Build diagrams from simple styled HTML; use HTML
  lists for lists of things.
- Use `<pre>` for code blocks. A custom-styled div must set
  `white-space: pre-wrap` (or `pre`), or the browser collapses all newlines

- Use callouts for key concepts, definitions, and important edge cases.
- Basic responsive styling so the page reads well on a phone.

A single self-contained HTML file: all CSS and JavaScript inline, with no
external runtime dependencies. Outbound source links are allowed; opening the
page itself must not fetch scripts, styles, fonts, images, or other assets.

Pull request explainer · COR-1185

A durable handoff for mirror creation

This pull request teaches the CLI to submit mirror creation as a persistent server-side request, poll that request until placement exists, and then reuse the existing clone-readiness poll. The old synchronous route remains the default while the new route rolls out.

PR #2207 21 changed files 7 reviewable commits Default-off rollout
01 · BackgroundWhy a long HTTP request is a fragile ownership boundary. 02 · IntuitionThe receipt-and-poll model, with concrete examples. 03 · CodeHow routing, polling, settings, and callers fit together. 04 · QuizFive questions that test the important constraints.

01 · Background

The problem begins with who owns the work

Know the mirror lifecycle already? Skip to “The narrow problem.”

Deep background: a mirror is created in two phases

Entire stores a repository in regional infrastructure. When the CLI asks for a mirror, the system first establishes a placement: a durable record saying which regional cluster owns the repository. The cluster then performs the slower work needed to make the Git repository usable. Those are different facts. A placement can exist while the clone is still being prepared.

The CLI therefore has to answer two questions in order: “Where will this mirror live?” and “Is that mirror ready yet?” The second question was already asynchronous before this pull request. After the server returned a placement, the CLI polled the mirror every two seconds until its state became ready or terminal.

The lifecycle the user cares about

Example: place entireio/cli in the us-east-2 cluster, then wait until it is cloneable.

CLI intententire repo mirror create
aws-us-east-2
→
Placementmirror_id = m_42
cluster = us-east-2
→
Preparationstate = cloning
→
Usable resultstate = ready
ssh://…/cli.git

This distinction matters because the command exposes --no-wait. “Do not wait” does not mean “fire an unvalidated packet and exit.” It means “wait until placement is known, print its URL, and leave clone readiness to the caller.” Without a placement there is no useful result to return.

The narrow problem: the first phase was still synchronous

Before this change, the CLI called the legacy mirror-create endpoint and kept that HTTP request open while the control plane arranged placement. If the connection disappeared, cancellation could propagate into work that the user expected the server to own. The client also had no durable request identifier it could poll after losing the original response.

The server-side contract added by entiredb PR #3441 (coreapi: add asynchronous mirror request routes) changes that boundary. Submission returns HTTP 202 and a Location header for a persistent request. The server can continue processing independently; the CLI follows the receipt until it contains a successful placement or a structured failure.

Before: connection owns phase one
  1. CLI opens POST /mirrors.
  2. Request stays open during placement.
  3. Response finally returns a mirror.
  4. CLI polls clone readiness.
After: request record owns phase one
  1. CLI opens POST /mirror-requests.
  2. Server returns 202 + Location.
  3. CLI polls the durable request.
  4. CLI reuses the same clone-readiness poll.
The governing invariant

After a successful submission, placement work belongs to the server-side request—not to the lifetime of the submitting HTTP connection.

Why this is a rollout bridge, not an endpoint replacement

COR-1185 (CLI: submit mirror creates through the async mirror-request routes) deliberately keeps both routes. A normal layered repository setting, async_mirror_requests, selects the new path. Its default is false, so existing repositories retain the synchronous behavior until a project or local override enables the new contract.

Once enabled, the choice is strict: the CLI does not probe for capability and does not fall back on a 404. A missing route is reported as a failure. In effect, that makes rollout errors visible instead of quietly converting an intended durability guarantee back into the legacy behavior.

// .entire/settings.json (shared project setting)
{
  "async_mirror_requests": true
}

// .entire/settings.local.json may override it for one clone.

This setting uses the repository’s ordinary project/local layering rather than a special local-only loader. There is one careful exception: entire repo mirror create is a control-plane command allowed to run even when the local .entire directory is broken. If settings cannot be loaded there, the command preserves that exemption and uses the default synchronous path rather than failing on local state.

02 · Intuition

Think of submission as getting a claim ticket

The essence is familiar from coat checks and job queues. Handing over the item is short. The receipt is durable. Collection can be retried. The new endpoint does not make placement itself instantaneous; it gives the client a stable name for work that continues after the first connection ends.

A concrete async request

The values are illustrative, but the state transitions match the generated API contract.

1. queuedPOST returns 202 and Location: /api/v1/mirror-requests/7b…
2. placingGET Location returns processing; the control plane still owns the job.
3. cloningThe request succeeds with mirror ID and URLs; the CLI enters its existing mirror poll.
4. readyThe mirror reports ready; the command prints the contract-backed URL.

The API request has four states—pending, processing, succeeded, and failed—but the CLI translates those into user-facing phases: queued, placing, and cloning. That translation keeps server vocabulary from leaking into every caller while still making progress intelligible.

One timeout budget crosses both polls

A subtle design choice follows from the claim-ticket model: --timeout is not reset after each phase. On the async path, a single context begins before submission and covers submission, placement polling, and clone polling. If the user asks for a 60-second wait, the entire operation gets 60 seconds—not 60 seconds for each step.

One wall-clock budget

Example only: the actual phase durations depend on the service.

0–1 ssubmit
→
1–12 spoll placement
→
12–47 spoll clone
→
47 sready within
60 s total

The command preserves the existing two-second clone poll cadence and its tolerance for fifteen consecutive poll errors—about thirty seconds. The placement poll uses the same bounded error pattern. This is especially important immediately after placement: authorization data can lag briefly, so an early 404 need not turn a successful placement into a failed command.

The Location header is both a receipt and a trust boundary

The CLI does not blindly fetch whatever URL appears in Location. It accepts only HTTP(S) URLs whose path is exactly a mirror-request resource with a UUID, and rejects user information, query strings, fragments, malformed paths, and scheme-relative hosts. That prevents a server response from turning the authenticated client into a general-purpose URL fetcher.

Cross-jurisdiction routing adds another wrinkle. A request may first contact one core, receive a 421 redirect signal, exchange credentials, and retry against the repository’s home core. The server can return a relative Location. The transport therefore anchors that location to the effective request URL after routing, so the poll goes to the same home core with the right token.

Why Location canonicalization belongs in the transport

The caller sees one trustworthy absolute poll target after cross-jurisdiction retry.

Initial targetcore A
control token
→
421 routinghome = core B
exchange token
→
202 responseLocation:
/api/v1/mirror-requests/7b…
→
Canonical targethttps://core-b/…/7b…

Truthful output beats a plausible guess

The legacy response tells the CLI whether the mirror was newly registered or already existed. The async success contract returns the mirror’s identity and URLs, but no equivalent “created” bit. The CLI therefore prints neutral language—Mirror placed at …—rather than guessing from circumstances. The URL is contract-backed; the creation history is not.

Important edge case

--no-wait on the async path still waits through placement. It skips only clone readiness, because the placement result is what provides the mirror URL.

03 · Code

The implementation keeps one orchestration path

The code is easiest to read as five cooperating layers. The generated API client describes the wire contract. Settings choose the rollout route. One orchestration function owns the lifecycle. Poll helpers interpret remote state. Finally, both the one-shot command and wizard call that same orchestration function.

1. Generate the contract instead of hand-writing HTTP

The OpenAPI specification now includes submission and lookup routes for mirror requests. Ogen generates request types, response variants, state enums, client methods, and JSON codecs. Most of the PR’s raw line count is this mechanical boundary; the handwritten code consumes typed outcomes rather than parsing unstructured responses.

The consequential contract is small: submission can yield 202 with a request plus Location; polling yields pending, processing, succeeded, or failed; success contains a mirror result; failure contains a stable code, message, and retryability flag. See the mirror-request routes in the pinned OpenAPI source.

// Conceptual wire exchange
POST /api/v1/mirror-requests
→ 202 Accepted
→ Location: /api/v1/mirror-requests/7b88…

GET /api/v1/mirror-requests/7b88…
→ { "status": "succeeded", "result": { "mirror_id": "m_42", … } }

2. Route at the command boundary, then forget the flag

The command loads normal layered settings and copies the boolean into mirrorCreateOptions. A settings-load error is deliberately non-fatal here because this control-plane command is exempt from the local .entire guard. After that boundary, callers pass one options value; they do not each reimplement rollout logic.

opts := mirrorCreateOptions{noWait: noWait, timeout: timeout}
if settings, err := LoadEntireSettings(cmd.Context()); err == nil {
    opts.async = settings.AsyncMirrorRequests
}

outcome, err := createAndAwaitMirror(ctx, client, owner, repo, cluster, opts)

The setting itself is merged by the same scalar-setting machinery as other booleans. A local false can override a project true, which matters when one developer or test environment must remain on the legacy route. The behavior is pinned by the layered-settings test.

3. Extend the lifecycle without duplicating its second half

createAndAwaitMirror is the center of the change. It selects only phase one: async submits and awaits a placement; sync calls the existing create method. Both branches then converge on the old clone-readiness poll and the same --no-wait behavior.

Control flow inside createAndAwaitMirror

The branch is narrow; placement results are normalized before common behavior resumes.

Setting false · legacy
  1. Call synchronous CreateMirror.
  2. Receive CreatedMirror.
  3. Preserve created/existing output.
Setting true · async
  1. Call CreateMirrorRequest.
  2. Validate and poll Location.
  3. Normalize success to CreatedMirror.
Common resultplacement + URLs
→
No wait?return placed URL
→
OtherwiseawaitMirrorReady
→
Reportready / failed / suspended

This convergence is the main maintainability win. The existing clone poll keeps its cadence, transient-error tolerance, and terminal-state handling. The new path adds a placement poll without creating a second version of everything that happens afterward.

4. Make remote uncertainty bounded and explicit

awaitMirrorPlacement performs three jobs: validate the poll target, translate request states, and bound transient failures. Pending and processing continue. Succeeded must include a usable mirror result. Failed preserves the server’s code and message and adds retry advice only when the server marks the failure retryable.

Network errors and short-lived authorization misses are tolerated, but not forever. Fifteen consecutive errors at a two-second interval exhaust the tolerance. A successful response resets the streak. Context cancellation remains silent, while deadline errors identify whether time expired during submission, placement, or readiness so the user knows what completed.

Observed stateCLI actionWhy
pending / processingContinue polling every 2 sThe server still owns live work.
succeeded + resultEnter clone poll or honor --no-waitPlacement now has a concrete URL.
failedReturn code + server detail; include retry advice when flaggedThe durable request reached a terminal business failure.
transient GET errorTolerate up to 15 consecutive failuresRouting and authorization can be briefly stale.
deadline exceededName the phase that timed outA generic timeout would hide whether submission succeeded.

5. Keep cross-jurisdiction repair below the orchestration

The request poller should not need to understand 421 responses, home-core discovery, or token exchange. The existing transport already owns those concerns. The PR extends that layer to canonicalize a successful async submission’s Location against the final request URL. That makes the generated response safe for ordinary callers to follow and keeps jurisdiction logic out of mirror orchestration.

The behavior is visible in the transport’s narrow canonicalization hook and its adjacent focused test.

6. Make one-shot and wizard differ only in presentation

The positional command creates one target and shows one spinner. The wizard may create several repository/region targets concurrently, with a limit of eight, and reports failures independently. Both now pass the same options into createAndAwaitMirror. The wizard installs a per-target phase callback, but it does not own a separate async implementation.

This shared path is tested in layers: focused tests exercise submission, status handling, Location validation, timeout and cancellation, cross-jurisdiction retry, settings selection, and output wording; a wizard test confirms concurrency remains bounded and one target’s failure does not cancel the rest. The main matrix lives in the async mirror request test file.

Verification evidence

The branch passed formatting, lint with zero issues, the race-enabled integration suite, 56 Vogon canaries, and 4 Roger canaries. Current-head Bugbot, Copilot, and Entire review findings were clean when the review cycle settled.

How the commits form independent review slices

The branch history mirrors the architecture: generated contract first, transport behavior next, then rollout configuration, shared runtime behavior, feedback corrections, precise timeout wording, and a final behavior-preserving simplification.

f35ce74b6a

Generate the mirror-request API client. Establishes typed wire shapes from OpenAPI.

d362936792

Canonicalize request locations. Keeps cross-jurisdiction polling on the effective home core.

68127e7d28

Add the rollout setting. Introduces the default-off route selector and layering tests.

18368324a9

Route mirror creation through async requests. Adds submission, placement polling, common lifecycle flow, and caller tests.

cd1a56de5b

Address review feedback. Makes the setting normally layered, preserves the broken-.entire exemption, retains unknown failure detail, and uses neutral async output.

f8511216e1

Clarify submission timeout wording. Distinguishes a timeout before receipt from one while polling placement.

1d65df23a2

Simplify the async flow. Reuses existing options, helpers, generated marshalers, and test setup without changing behavior.

The resulting PR #2207 (Submit mirror creates through async request routes) is therefore not “replace one POST with another.” It moves phase-one ownership to a durable server record while deliberately preserving the CLI’s established phase-two behavior, caller structure, and rollout escape hatch.

04 · Quiz

Check the model, not the symbol names

Each question has one best answer. Choose an option to reveal the explanation.

1. An async create has a 60-second timeout. Placement succeeds after 45 seconds. How much fresh timeout does clone readiness receive?

2. The repository enables async requests, but its target service lacks the route. What should the CLI do?

3. Why does async one-shot output say “Mirror placed at …” instead of “Mirror registered at …”?

4. What does --no-wait skip on the async path?

5. Why is a relative Location canonicalized in the cross-jurisdiction transport?

<skill>
<name>pfleidi:task-validate</name>
<path>/Users/pfleidi/.agents/skills/pfleidi/skills/task-validate/SKILL.md</path>
---
name: task-validate
description: >
  Perform isolated final validation of one implemented Linear or GitHub task
  against its live exit criteria and the full approved commit range. Use a
  temporary Entire worktree and, when already under Herdr, a dedicated
  validation tab and agent that can report code failures to the implementation
  agent.
---

# Task Validation

Independently validate one implementation without modifying it. The live task's
exit criteria are the source of truth. Handoffs, comments, commit messages, and
implementation claims are context to verify, not authority.

Herdr enhances this workflow but is not required. Use it only when
`HERDR_ENV=1` and the Herdr CLI is available. Otherwise perform the same
isolated checks in the invoking session and omit peer-agent communication.

This skill applies only to committed repository changes. For a decision,
investigation, tracker-only task, or operational validation with no repository
change, use `task-implement`'s no-code path and do not create a validation
branch or worktree.

This isolated local validation owns important correctness, edge cases, error
paths, and scenarios that require internal control or fault injection. Prefer
automated tests that also run in CI. If required coverage is missing, report it
to implementation as a test gap; do not substitute a manual staging or
production procedure. A separate deployed validation, when needed, follows the
customer-surface rules in `task-implement`.

## Preconditions

Do not start validation until all of these are true:

- The implementation has one or more commits explicitly approved by the user.
- The implementation worktree is clean.
- The base commit and implementation head are known.
- The live task and its current exit criteria can be read.

Resolve and retain the full approved implementation-head SHA. When under Herdr,
capture the current coordinator target and its workspace, tab, and pane IDs.
List live agents, resolve the expected implementation name from the same task-ID
normalization used by `task-implement`, and inspect that actual agent. Verify
that it owns this task and capture its live name, pane, and workspace IDs. If
the match is missing or ambiguous, stop rather than reconstructing a target.

Validate the complete `base...head` change, not only the latest commit. If the
issue criteria are contradictory, stale, or not testable, return Blocked with
the exact issue edit or decision needed. Do not reinterpret them in the
handover.

## Isolate The Run

Create a fresh temporary branch named for the task and implementation head, such
as `validate/<task-id>-<short-sha>`. Validate the generated name with `git
check-ref-format --branch`, confirm that it does not already exist, and create
it explicitly at the full approved head SHA. Create its worktree with `entire
worktree create <branch> --existing-branch`, passing the branch as one quoted
argument. Never reuse a prior validation worktree.

Before starting validation, verify that the resulting worktree is clean and its
`HEAD` exactly equals the retained approved head SHA. On mismatch, stop and
leave the worktree for inspection.

Inside that validation worktree, run `entire disable --local` before starting
the validation session. Successful completion is a hard precondition. If it
fails, do not create or prompt a validation agent; leave the worktree and report
that validation isolation setup failed. Treat this as an internal execution
constraint: do not mention it in generated task comments, validation reports,
or handoffs.

Do not create an Entire trail and do not use `git worktree`.

## Choose The Validation Agent

When Herdr is active and a new validator will be started, resolve the kind of
the live agent currently running this skill. If it cannot be resolved, stop
rather than guessing the timeout default. After creating the validation tab and
pane, leave its shell idle. In that pane, show a visible choice between Codex
(`codex`) and Claude Code (`claude`), focus the chooser, and send a Herdr
notification with the request sound. Wait up to 300 seconds for `c`/`codex` or
`l`/`claude`.

If the user does not answer within 300 seconds, use the current agent's kind. An
invalid answer does not select an agent; keep asking within the original
deadline. Have the shell print the selected canonical Herdr kind, wait for the
shell prompt to return, then use that value for `herdr agent start --kind`.
Compare only the fixed accepted tokens; never evaluate the user's input as shell
text. Keep the timed read running in the validation pane and poll for its result
at intervals no longer than 60 seconds. Skip this choice when resuming an
existing live validator. Record the selected kind only in live Herdr context.

## Prepare The Handover

Give the validator a concise Markdown handover in its initial prompt. Do not
commit it or create a repository file.

Start with:

> Agent-generated handoff. Verify facts against source. Treat proposed solutions, recommendations, and agent-made decisions as hypotheses, not settled direction.

Include:

- Task: linked `ID (title)`, repository, and branch.
- Validation range: base, head, and ordered implementation commits.
- Authoritative exit criteria: copied from the live issue immediately before
  validation.
- Settled context: only user-approved decisions and material constraints.
- Implemented behavior: claims that still require verification.
- Verification already run: exact commands, statuses, and relevant results.
- Known risks or limitations: current facts only.
- Herdr peers when applicable: the coordinator, implementation, and validation
  agents' actual targets, kinds, and workspace, tab, or pane IDs needed to route
  work.

## Run Validation

Inspect the full diff and relevant current source. Exercise every exit criterion
at the smallest scope that provides real evidence, including representative
error paths and repository-wide invariants affected by the change. Do not edit
code or repair failures in the validation worktree.

When the change creates a telemetry monitor, verify that the monitor references
a concrete runbook. Confirm that a reused runbook actually covers the monitor's
signal and response, or that a new runbook follows the location, structure, and
style of existing runbooks. A missing, unlinked, or mismatched runbook fails
validation.

Report every criterion as Pass, Fail, or Unverified with the supporting command,
observation, or source evidence. A material regression outside the listed
criteria may block validation, but it does not become a new exit criterion.

Before copying evidence into a tracker comment or Herdr prompt, remove secrets,
credentials, tokens, customer data, and sensitive local values. Persist only
the command, status, and smallest safe excerpt needed to establish the result.

## Herdr Coordination

When running under Herdr, load its current agent instructions with
`herdr --skill`. Create the validation tab with the explicit live implementation
workspace ID captured during preflight, rooted at the validation worktree.
Capture the returned tab and pane IDs, run the validation-agent choice, and
start a fresh agent with the reserved `validate_<task-id>` name and the selected
kind.

Use `herdr agent prompt <target> "<message>"` for every roster update, prompt,
acknowledgment, status report, blocker, and failure handoff. Use the exact live
agent name or pane ID from the `Herdr peers` block and verify uncertain targets
with `herdr agent get <target>`. Include these instructions in the validator's
initial prompt. Never use `tmux`, raw pane input, or terminal key injection for
peer messages. If Herdr rejects a target or prompt, do not fall back to another
transport; preserve the error and follow the relevant blocked path below.

Build one live `Herdr peers` block containing the task ID; coordinator target,
kind, and workspace; implementation agent name, kind, workspace, and pane; and
validation agent name, kind, tab, and pane. Give it to the validator. Before
prompting validation work, send the implementation agent a short roster update
containing the actual validator and coordinator targets. If Herdr rejects that
update, do not start validation. If the coordinator and implementation roles
are the same live agent, record the combined role in the peer block and skip the
self-prompt.

Prompt the validator through `herdr agent prompt` with the handover and wait for
it to settle. Then read the named validator's output; lifecycle state alone is
not the report. Tell the validator to send a short completion or blocker
notification to the coordinator target with `herdr agent prompt` while leaving
the full evidence in its own response.

If validation proves that a code change is required:

- Add a concise issue comment naming the failed exit criteria and evidence,
  starting with the repository's agent-generated handoff marker.
- Prompt the implementation agent with the issue-comment link and validation
  base and head. Identify the validation agent as the sender and the coordinator
  as the acknowledgment target. Describe the observed gap without prescribing a
  repair unless the exit criterion does.
- Wait for the implementation agent to settle, read its response, and verify an
  explicit acknowledgment before cleanup.

If the implementation agent is absent, blocked, or no longer owns its pane,
leave the durable issue comment, keep the validation worktree, and report the
path to the user. Do not start a replacement agent.

Environment failures, flaky checks, and unclear criteria are not code-change
requests. Keep the validation tab available and return the blocker to the user.

Without Herdr, report failures directly to the user and in the issue comment.
Do not attempt agent discovery or forwarding.

## Finish And Clean Up

On success, record concise evidence in the issue, starting with the repository's
agent-generated handoff marker, and state which native next transition is ready.
Do not close the issue merely because local validation passed when merge,
deployment, rollout, or post-deploy proof remains.

If the remaining proof can only be created by a later project issue that this
task does not own, report a mis-scoped exit criterion instead of treating an
indefinite wait as validation progress. Recommend task alignment or project
reconciliation so the criterion can move to the rollout, enablement, or
integration issue that owns its prerequisite.

Close only the validation tab created by this run. Remove only the validation
worktree created by this run, only when clean, using Entire without force. Then
delete the temporary branch with non-forcing `git branch -d`. If cleanup refuses
or the worktree is dirty, leave it intact and report the exact path.

A failed validation that the implementation agent acknowledged may be cleaned
up after its evidence is durable. Each retry starts from newly approved commits
in a fresh validation worktree.

## Tracker References

In human-facing prose, render every issue or pull request as `ID (title)` and
link the whole label when a URL exists. Never show a bare tracker ID or issue/PR
URL. Raw IDs remain valid in commands, API fields, branches, paths, and internal
identifiers.

</skill>

{"id":"COR-1185","title":"CLI: submit mirror creates through the async mirror-request routes","description":"## Problem

`entire repo mirror create` currently calls `CreateMirror`, waits for a synchronous `CreatedMirror`, and only then polls the mirror status until the initial clone is ready. From Sydney or Mumbai the first of those two waits measured 12–15 seconds under the old 15s gateway wall — and 26.9s (AU) / 28.9s (IN) once that wall was lifted on 2026-08-18 (<pull-request id="4a2e3909-6a1d-472f-9bb5-37b1cd378920" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/review/entire-core-gateway-request-timeout-30s-45s-sized-off-measured-latency-ecc0fc64f07d">entirehq/fleet#4613</pull-request>) — and a caller timeout during it can leave a half-applied placement behind.

[COR-1181](<https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1181>) adds a route that accepts a create and returns immediately: `POST /api/v1/mirror-requests` → **202** with a `Location` pointing at a pollable request resource. This issue moves the CLI onto it.

Both the one-shot command and the wizard already share `createAndAwaitMirror`. Keep that single path — the CLI has been bitten before by the two drifting apart.

## What this is, and is not

It is a route switch, not a response-shape migration. `POST /api/v1/mirrors` is never modified, and the server never sends a 202 to a caller that asked for the old route. There is no header to send, no capability to advertise, and no branching on which response came back. Each invocation selects one route from the setting.

The CLI keeps both routes during rollout behind the `async_mirror_requests` setting, resolved like any **regular layered setting** (amended 2026-08-31, review decision on trail 1195 — supersedes the local-only alignment decision). Unset or false uses the existing synchronous route; true selects the async route.

There is no capability preflight and no automatic fallback. If the setting selects the async route against a core that does not serve it, fail loudly. A submission-level 404 is not a reliable capability signal because the live route can also return existence-agnostic repository failures.

The setting prevents accidental adoption; it does not prove the backend can complete accepted work. Enable the async path for normal use only after every production region serves the route and its mirror-create consumer is enabled.

## A real simplification

**Resubmitting is safe.** The new route enforces one live request per (provider, owner, repo, cluster); a resubmission returns the *existing* request's 202 and `Location` rather than starting a second placement. So a transport failure before acceptance can simply be retried, rather than needing the careful "did that write land?" reasoning the current code carries.

## Work

**Regenerate the client** for the [COR-1205](<https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1205>) contract.

Give `createAndAwaitMirror` **two explicit phases:**

1. Submit the request and poll it until placement succeeds or terminally fails.
2. With the mirror id from phase one, continue the existing mirror-status poll until the initial clone is ready.

Keep the existing phase-two poll unchanged: `GET /api/v1/mirrors/{mirrorId}` every two seconds with the current bound of 15 consecutive errors (about 30 seconds). After phase one succeeds, the first mirror read can return 404 for roughly five seconds because the SpiceDB `minimize_latency` reverse lookup is not read-after-write consistent. That behavior was accepted on <issue id="6624dff2-dd8d-481e-95a0-abcf39a5d272" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1337/staging-validation-cycle-for-the-async-mirror-create-dispatch-path">COR-1337</issue> and is already covered by the current bound; retry it rather than treating the first 404 as terminal. The manual staging script needed the same bounded retry.

**Carry over the cross-jurisdiction machinery.** The new route returns the same 421 with `home_core_url` for a cluster outside the core's jurisdiction, so the existing cross-jurisdiction round-tripper and token exchange need pointing at the new route, not rebuilding.

Keep `--no-wait` **honest.** It skips waiting for the clone; it does **not** return on a bare acceptance. It still waits until placement is registered and a real mirror id and URL can be printed — which means polling phase one to completion. Worth stating plainly: `--no-wait` does not get dramatically faster, because the work it waits on is the work that was slow. What improves is that the wait is now interruptible and resumable rather than a held-open connection that strands state when it drops.

**Make the progress display legible across both phases.** "Queued", "placing" and "cloning" are different states and a user watching an operation this long deserves to know which one they are in.

Define `--wait-timeout` **over the full placement-plus-clone wait**, unless the upstream contract forces separate deadlines.

**Preserve** bounded wizard concurrency, independent per-repository and per-region failures, and the existing handling for already-existing or suspended placements.

**Render terminal failures** using the stable code and message from the request resource, mapped onto the existing actionable errors rather than a generic "polling failed".

**Validate the selected path end to end.** Against staging, run a release-candidate CLI through one-shot waited success, `--no-wait`, and wizard creation using synthetic repositories. Before public production release, run normal CLI creation through each production region after its consumer is enabled, plus one wizard run to prove that caller path. A passing run prints a real mirror id and URL, reaches clone readiness when requested, and leaves no request nonterminal beyond the bounded wait. Never use customer repositories or data.

## Boundary — decided upstream 2026-08-19, amended 2026-08-31

> Amended 2026-08-31 to match the shipped contract (entiredb #3441): failures may arrive **synchronously at submit or as polled terminal states** — handle both. A mistyped or inaccessible repo now fails at submit with an existence-agnostic error, and an already-existing mirror on the target cluster returns 409 at submit. Render the terminal codes — `repo_inaccessible`, `github_link_required`, `source_too_large`, `github_unavailable`, `mirror_url_conflict`, `mirror_conflict`, `placement_deleted`, `mirror_name_conflict`, `invalid_request`, `internal` — as actionable errors, honour the `retryable` flag from the response when suggesting a retry, and treat unknown codes as a generic terminal failure.

## Acceptance criteria

* One-shot and wizard creation still share one `createAndAwaitMirror` implementation.
* Accepted → placement success → mirror ready produces a success output with the mirror id and URL; the async path prints neutral wording, since the contract carries no created/found distinction (decided 2026-08-31).
* `--no-wait` returns once placement is registered with a printable mirror id and URL, and does not wait for cloning.
* Accepted → terminal placement failure exits non-zero with an actionable error, not a generic poll failure.
* Cancellation and `--wait-timeout` stop both polls cleanly, and a cancelled CLI does not cancel the server-side placement.
* Transient poll failures follow a bounded retry policy; a malformed or missing `Location` fails loudly.
* A resubmission after a transport failure converges on one placement.
* Cross-jurisdiction creation still routes to the home core and completes.
* The async-route setting is unset/false by default, resolves like any regular layered setting (amended 2026-08-31), and preserves the synchronous route; true selects the async route. There is no availability preflight or fallback, and an unavailable selected route fails loudly.
* Normal async-path enablement is gated on every production region serving the route and running the mirror-create consumer.
* Shared `createAndAwaitMirror` tests cover success, synchronous submit failure, terminal polled failure, unknown failure codes, retryable guidance, transient failures in both poll phases, cancellation in both phases, the full-operation timeout, `--no-wait`, malformed or missing `Location`, resubmission after transport failure, the initial phase-two 404 window, and existing or suspended placement behavior.
* Focused one-shot and wizard tests prove that both callers use the shared path and preserve their own output, progress, result folding, bounded concurrency, and independent per-repository/per-region failures; they do not duplicate the full shared scenario matrix.

## Dependencies

[COR-1205](<https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1205>) is merged and its contract is frozen, so CLI implementation intentionally begins ahead of the BFF. Shipping still follows the BFF ([COR-1184](<https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1184>)); the setting remains off for normal use until the BFF path has carried production traffic and every production region serves the route with its mirror-create consumer ---
name: herdr
description: "Control Herdr, a terminal multiplexer for coding agents. Use only when the user explicitly mentions Herdr or asks to use Herdr to inspect or control panes, tabs, workspaces, commands, or another agent. Do not use merely because a task could benefit from a background terminal, delegation, or parallel work. Requires HERDR_ENV=1."
---

# Herdr

Herdr organizes terminals into workspaces, tabs, and panes, recognizes coding agents running inside panes, and exposes the current session through the `herdr` CLI.

Before issuing any control command, verify that this agent is running inside a Herdr-managed pane:

```bash
test "${HERDR_ENV:-}" = 1
```

If the check fails, say that you are not running inside Herdr and stop. Do not inspect or control the focused Herdr session from outside Herdr.

When the check passes, the `herdr` binary in `PATH` talks to the current session. Use it to inspect neighboring work, create terminal layout, start agents and commands, read output, and wait for state changes.

## Learn the current CLI

The installed binary is the authority for command syntax. Start with:

```bash
herdr --help
```

Then print the relevant command group by running the group without a subcommand:

```bash
herdr agent
herdr pane
herdr workspace
herdr tab
herdr worktree
herdr terminal
herdr notification
herdr integration
herdr session
```

Do not run bare `herdr` for discovery; it launches or attaches the TUI. Do not probe a mutating nested command by omitting arguments. Commands such as `herdr workspace create` are valid with defaults and will execute.

Most control commands return JSON. Read identifiers and state from those responses instead of predicting them.

## Understand layout, panes, and agents

Choose the primitive that matches the job:

- Workspace, tab, and pane topology organize terminal locations.
- Pane commands control raw terminals, shells, tests, servers, input, and output.
- Agent commands control the recognized coding agent currently occupying a pane.

A pane exists whether or not it contains an agent. `agent start` requires an existing available shell pane and never creates, splits, or moves layout. Use pane commands for ordinary processes. Use agent commands when Herdr must validate agent identity or interpret `idle`, `working`, `blocked`, `done`, and `unknown` lifecycle states.

Agent commands accept either a unique live agent name or the pane ID currently hosting that agent. They do not accept terminal IDs or bare agent-kind labels. Names must match `[a-z][a-z0-9_-]{0,31}` and be unique among live agents. A name follows the current pane occupant and is cleared when that agent exits, is released, or is replaced.

`idle` means the agent is ready for input and its tab has been seen in the focused Herdr UI. `done` is the same underlying idle state after unseen background work finishes. Focusing the tab or targeting the pane or agent with a focus command marks it seen. CLI reads do not mark it seen. `blocked` means Herdr recognized an approval or question UI. `unknown` means an agent is present but Herdr cannot classify it confidently; it does not prove completion.

## Use IDs and caller context

Public IDs are opaque stable handles:

- workspace: `w1`
- tab: `w1:t1`
- pane: `w1:p1`

Closed tab and pane IDs are not reused. A pane moved into another workspace receives a new workspace-qualified pane ID. After `pane move`, continue with `.result.move_result.pane.pane_id` or the live agent name. The old value is reported as `.result.move_result.previous_pane_id`; only the moved process's inherited caller context keeps resolving that old ID, so do not use it as a general agent target.

Herdr injects the caller's context into each managed pane:

```bash
printf '%s\n' "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID" "$HERDR_TAB_ID" "$HERDR_PANE_ID"
```

Prefer `--current` when a pane command should target the calling pane. Omitting a target may use the UI-focused pane, which can belong to the user or another client.

Discover live state with:

```bash
herdr workspace list
herdr tab list --workspace "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID"
herdr pane current --current
herdr pane list --workspace "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID"
herdr agent list
```

Creation responses expose the IDs to use next. `workspace create` returns `.result.workspace`, `.result.tab`, and `.result.root_pane`. `tab create` returns `.result.tab` and `.result.root_pane`. `pane split` returns the new pane as `.result.pane`.

## Start and coordinate an agent

Default to a sibling pane in the current tab and the current working directory. Do not create a workspace, tab, worktree, or different cwd unless the user explicitly requests that topology or location.

Honor a direction requested by the user. Otherwise inspect the caller pane:

```bash
herdr pane layout --pane "$HERDR_PANE_ID"
```

Split a wide pane to the right and a narrow or tall pane down. Avoid repeated same-direction splits that create unusably narrow columns or short rows. Keep the user's focus in the calling pane and explicitly preserve the caller's working directory:

```bash
herdr pane split --current --direction right --cwd "$PWD" --no-focus
```

Replace `right` with `down` when appropriate. Read the new pane ID from `.result.pane.pane_id`.

An available shell pane must be at its interactive prompt, with the shell itself in the foreground and no foreground command, editor, or agent running. Start a supported agent in that pane with a useful unique name:

```bash
herdr agent start reviewer --kind codex --pane <returned-pane-id>
```

Use the kind requested by the user. Run `herdr agent` to inspect the installed kind list and options. Pass native agent arguments only after `--`:

```bash
herdr agent start reviewer --kind codex --pane <returned-pane-id> -- <agent-args...>
```

A successful `agent start` returns only after Herdr detects the expected agent in the same pane and considers it ready for interactive input. If the agent is blocked during startup, the command returns `agent_not_ready` immediately but keeps the name available for `agent read` and `agent send-keys`. Wait until the agent becomes idle before prompting it. Startup defaults to a 30-second timeout.

Submit work through the agent surface:

```bash
herdr agent prompt reviewer "Review the current diff and report only actionable findings." --wait --timeout 120000
```

`agent prompt` honors the pane's live bracketed-paste mode and sends text followed by encoded Enter after a short delay. It rejects an agent already waiting at an approval or question dialog with `agent_blocked` before sending any input. Inspect the blocked UI and ask the user before answering it. For normal agent work, `--wait` is enough: it waits for the first settled `idle`, `done`, or `blocked` state. Do not repeat those defaults with `--until`.

A prompt sent from a non-working state must produce an observed lifecycle change within five seconds. Otherwise Herdr returns `agent_prompt_stalled` instead of waiting indefinitely. This wait tracks lifecycle state, not an individual turn; if the agent is already working, completion of the active turn may satisfy it.

Use `--until` only for a state-specific workflow, such as waiting for an already-running agent to request input:

```bash
herdr agent wait reviewer --until blocked --timeout 120000
```

Without `--until`, standalone `agent wait` uses the same settled-state defaults as `agent prompt --wait`.

Use logical keys for interactive agent UI controls:

```bash
herdr agent send-keys reviewer esc
herdr agent send-keys reviewer ctrl+c
```

Herdr validates all keys before writing any bytes. Read the result through the resolved agent:

```bash
herdr agent get reviewer
herdr agent read reviewer --source recent-unwrapped --lines 120
```

If a wait fails or returns `blocked`, inspect `agent get` and `agent read` before deciding what input to send. Use the pane surface only when raw terminal control is intentional.

## Run an ordinary command in another pane

Create a sibling pane with the same geometry rule, preserve the caller's working directory, and keep user focus unchanged:

```bash
herdr pane split --current --direction right --cwd "$PWD" --no-focus
```

Read the new pane ID from `.result.pane.pane_id`, then run and inspect the command:

```bash
herdr pane run <returned-pane-id> "just test"
herdr pane wait-output <returned-pane-id> --match "test result" --timeout 120000
herdr pane read <returned-pane-id> --source recent-unwrapped --lines 120
```

`pane run` atomically sends command text and Enter. `pane wait-output` searches the selected snapshot immediately, so output that already exists can match. Use `--match <text>` for a literal substring or `--regex <pattern>` for a Rust regular expression. Omitting `--timeout` allows an indefinite wait.

Use the read source that matches the task:

- `visible`: the currently rendered viewport.
- `recent`: recent rendered output, including soft wraps.
- `recent-unwrapped`: recent output with soft wraps joined; prefer it for logs and transcripts.
- `detection`: the plain-text bottom-buffer snapshot used for agent detection.

Use `--format ansi` when colors and terminal styling are evidence. Otherwise use text.

`--lines` asks Herdr for more rows from the pane's available screen and host scrollback. If increasing it does not reveal more of a completed response, the pane is probably running the agent on the terminal's alternate screen. Rows that leave the alternate screen do not enter Herdr's host scrollback, so a larger line count cannot recover them.

After that failed read, ask the agent to write its complete response as Markdown in a temporary directory and reply only with the file path, then read the file directly. Use this only as a fallback; do not request file output in the initial prompt.

## Safety and coordination rules

- Use `--no-focus` for background work unless the user asked to switch context.
- Use `--current`, an explicit pane ID, or a unique agent name. Do not rely on another client's focused pane.
- Parse IDs from JSON responses. Do not derive them from sidebar order or examples.
- Do not close workspaces, tabs, panes, or sessions you did not create unless the user explicitly asked.
- Never run `herdr server stop` from an active session unless the user explicitly intends to stop the server and its pane processes.
- Never kill the main Herdr process. Use named test sessions for experiments that need an isolated server.
- CLI server errors are JSON on stderr with exit status 1. CLI syntax errors exit with status 2.

---
name: testing
description: >
  Local testing strategy and review guidance for meaningful tests, choosing unit vs integration vs end-to-end scope,
  avoiding production-only test seams and over-mocking, and keeping test helpers readable, especially in Go.
  Use when writing, changing, or reviewing tests; adding mocks or test helpers; deciding test scope; or when user mentions pfleidi:testing.
---

# Testing Guidance

## Core Principle

Tests should make changed behavior trustworthy without distorting production code. Prefer behavior and contracts over implementation details. Use the smallest scope that gives real confidence.

## Never Use Real Customer Data

**NEVER put real customer data in test cases.** No production records, real PII, real emails, real account/customer IDs, or scrubbed copies of live data — "anonymized" or "scrubbed" production data is still forbidden. Fabricate synthetic fixtures that exercise the same shape and edge cases. When reviewing, reject any test carrying real customer data outright.

## Choose Test Scope

- **Unit tests** - pure logic, parsing, validation, small components, and behavior with explicit dependencies that can be supplied naturally.
- **Integration tests** - real wiring, filesystem, config, databases, process boundaries, generated code, framework behavior, or cases where unit isolation would require awkward mocks or production-only seams.
- **End-to-end / smoke tests** - critical user or system flows across process or service boundaries. Keep these few, stable, and high value.

Cover changed behavior, important edge cases, and error paths. Do not chase line coverage with brittle tests that only exercise private structure.

## Preserve Test Layers

Unit, integration, and end-to-end suites are complementary layers with different costs. A fast unit suite may intentionally skip real wiring, config, databases, filesystems, generated code, or framework behavior when another suite owns that boundary. That is not incomplete unit testing; it is a useful split of responsibilities.

Before changing test scope, identify the missing confidence:

- If the gap is pure logic, parsing, validation, or small behavior with natural dependencies, add or adjust a unit test.
- If the gap is real wiring, config loading, filesystem/database behavior, generated code, process boundaries, or framework behavior, first check existing integration/e2e coverage. If coverage is missing, add a narrow integration/e2e test at that boundary.
- Preserve useful fast unit tests. Do not rewrite broad unit test suites into integration tests just to cover wiring. Convert a unit test only when its stated subject is wrong and an additive test at the right layer would not cover the gap.

## Avoid Production Test Seams

Do not add production code that exists only to make tests easier:

- Mutable function variables swapped in tests.
- Mutable package-wide settings changed by tests.
- Exported `Reset`, `Set`, or hook functions only used by tests.
- Global clocks, filesystems, HTTP clients, env readers, or command runners added only for unit tests.

If a test needs these, prefer dependency injection through existing construction paths, small typed interfaces around external effects, or a higher-scope integration test.

## Test Helpers

Helpers are useful when they make the test shorter and easier to understand. They are harmful when they hide the behavior being tested.

Use a helper when:

- It removes noisy setup or cleanup that is not the point of the test.
- Its name is domain-specific and explains what the caller gets.
- The test remains understandable without opening the helper.
- It preserves the important inputs, expected values, and assertions at the call site.

Inline the code instead when:

- The helper saves only a few lines but hides the arrange/act/assert flow.
- The reviewer must inspect the helper to know what behavior is asserted.
- The helper takes booleans, loose maps, or option bags that obscure intent.
- The helper embeds important defaults, expected values, or failure conditions.
- The helper is generic test plumbing with no domain meaning.

Prefer local helpers in the test file until reuse is clear. Moving helpers to shared test utilities raises the readability bar because future readers lose locality.

## Go-Specific Helper Rules

- Prefer table-driven tests or `t.Run` subtests when repeated cases share the same logic. Each table row should be a complete scenario with inputs, expected outputs, and a clear name.
- Keep expected values in the table row or test body. Do not hide them in helper defaults.
- Use `t.Run` names to identify cases, then keep failure messages focused on `got` vs `want`.
- If a helper can fail the test, accept `testing.TB` or `*testing.T` and call `t.Helper()` first so failures point to the caller.
- Use `t.Cleanup`, `t.TempDir`, and `t.Setenv` for resource setup when appropriate. Remember that process-wide changes such as environment or current-directory changes are not safe for parallel tests unless the testing API says so.
- Return concrete values from builders. Avoid global shared fixtures and mutable package state.
- Avoid generic assertion helpers unless they are clearly domain-specific. A direct `if got != want { t.Fatalf(...) }` is often more readable than an abstraction.

## Review Checklist

When writing or reviewing tests, flag:

- Changed behavior, edge cases, or error paths without meaningful coverage.
- Tests that prove private implementation details instead of behavior.
- Unit tests used where real wiring/config/filesystem/database/framework behavior is the confidence boundary.
- Review feedback that tries to replace useful unit tests with integration tests instead of adding a narrow integration/e2e test for a proven uncovered boundary.
- Helpers that force readers to leave the test to understand the scenario.
- Helpers that hide expected values, assertions, or important defaults.
- Production-only seams introduced to make tests pass.
- Broad mocks where an integration test would be simpler and more trustworthy.
- Real customer data in fixtures — production records, real PII, real IDs, or scrubbed copies of live data. Reject outright.

## Source Basis

This guidance is synthesized from Go's testing package documentation, Go's subtests guidance, and the Go table-driven tests wiki, plus local preferences about avoiding production-only test seams.

## Tracker References

In human-facing prose, render every issue or pull request as `ID (title)` and
link the whole label when a URL exists. Never show a bare tracker ID or issue/PR
URL. Raw IDs remain valid in commands, API fields, branches, paths, and internal
identifiers.

- **Integration tests** - real wiring, filesystem, config, databases, process boundaries, generated code, framework behavior, or cases where unit isolation would require awkward mocks or production-only seams.
- **End-to-end / smoke tests** - critical user or system flows across process or service boundaries. Keep these few, stable, and high value.

Cover changed behavior, important edge cases, and error paths. Do not chase line coverage with brittle tests that only exercise private structure.

## Preserve Test Layers

Unit, integration, and end-to-end suites are complementary layers with different costs. A fast unit suite may intentionally skip real wiring, config, databases, filesystems, generated code, or framework behavior when another suite owns that boundary. That is not incomplete unit testing; it is a useful split of responsibilities.

Before changing test scope, identify the missing confidence:

- If the gap is pure logic, parsing, validation, or small behavior with natural dependencies, add or adjust a unit test.
- If the gap is real wiring, config loading, filesystem/database behavior, generated code, process boundaries, or framework behavior, first check existing integration/e2e coverage. If coverage is missing, add a narrow integration/e2e test at that boundary.
- Preserve useful fast unit tests. Do not rewrite broad unit test suites into integration tests just to cover wiring. Convert a unit test only when its stated subject is wrong and an additive test at the right layer would not cover the gap.

Do not add production code that exists only to make tests easier:

- Mutable function variables swapped in tests.
- Mutable package-wide settings changed by tests.
- Exported `Reset`, `Set`, or hook functions only used by tests.
- Global clocks, filesystems, HTTP clients, env readers, or command runners added only for unit tests.

If a test needs these, prefer dependency injection through existing construction paths, small typed interfaces around external effects, or a higher-scope integration test.

## Test Helpers

Helpers are useful when they make the test shorter and easier to understand. They are harmful when they hide the behavior being tested.

Use a helper when:

- It removes noisy setup or cleanup that is not the point of the test.
- Its name is domain-specific and explains what the caller gets.
- The test remains understandable without opening the helper.
- It preserves the important inputs, expected values, and assertions at the call site.

Inline the code instead when:

- The helper saves only a few lines but hides the arrange/act/assert flow.
- The reviewer must inspect the helper to know what behavior is asserted.
- The helper takes booleans, loose maps, or option bags that obscure intent.
- The helper embeds important defaults, expected values, or failure conditions.
- The helper is generic test plumbing with no domain meaning.

Prefer local helpers in the test file until reuse is clear. Moving helpers to shared test utilities raises the readability bar because future readers lose locality.

## Go-Specific Helper Rules

- Prefer table-driven tests or `t.Run` subtests when repeated cases share the same logic. Each table row should be a complete scenario with inputs, expected outputs, and a clear name.
- Keep expected values in the table row or test body. Do not hide them in helper defaults.
- Use `t.Run` names to identify cases, then keep failure messages focused on `got` vs `want`.
- If a helper can fail the test, accept `testing.TB` or `*testing.T` and call `t.Helper()` first so failures point to the caller.
- Use `t.Cleanup`, `t.TempDir`, and `t.Setenv` for resource setup when appropriate. Remember that process-wide changes such as environment or current-directory changes are not safe for parallel tests unless the testing API says so.
- Return concrete values from builders. Avoid global shared fixtures and mutable package state.
- Avoid generic assertion helpers unless they are clearly domain-specific. A direct `if got != want { t.Fatalf(...) }` is often more readable than an abstraction.

## Review Checklist

When writing or reviewing tests, flag:

- Changed behavior, edge cases, or error paths without meaningful coverage.
- Tests that prove private implementation details instead of behavior.
- Unit tests used where real wiring/config/filesystem/database/framework behavior is the confidence boundary.
- Review feedback that tries to replace useful unit tests with integration tests instead of adding a narrow integration/e2e test for a proven uncovered boundary.
- Helpers that force readers to leave the test to understand the scenario.
- Helpers that hide expected values, assertions, or important defaults.
- Production-only seams introduced to make tests pass.
- Broad mocks where an integration test would be simpler and more trustworthy.
- Real customer data in fixtures — production records, real PII, real IDs, or scrubbed copies of live data. Reject outright.

link the whole label when a URL exists. Never show a bare tracker ID or issue/PR
URL. Raw IDs remain valid in commands, API fields, branches, paths, and internal
identifiers.
